### From the web-UI and tooling-language questions (session 7)

Asked together: *"should `.dacode/plans/…md` be accessible via the web UI,
especially in server mode?"* and *"we might not want to use/rely on python … as
much as we can — build rust-based functions."* The second became decision **B16**
and delta **A20**; the first is answered below and recorded in
[32](part2-engine/32-task-tracking.md) and as an interaction note on A7 — three
places, because §16.6 was lost by being in only the spec.

- [x] **U55 · The live task tree already works in server mode and needs nothing.** It is
      folded into `Snapshot.tasks` (§3.5) and the fold is shared code in
      `dacode-protocol`, so TUI, web, extensions and a remote `attach` all render
      the same tree with **no new protocol surface**. That is principle 1 paying
      for itself, and it is worth stating plainly because the question reads as
      bigger than it is.
- [x] **U56 · ✅ CLOSED 2026-09-19 by A7 — all three gaps, and the answer to (1) is not
      the one this item guessed at.** *The promoted board is the real gap*: a board is a
      file in the repo, not session state, so a browser talking to a remote `serve` (§8.1)
      cannot read it from disk.
      1. ~~**No screen for it.**~~ → **It has a screen and a route, and the route is
         repo-scoped rather than project-scoped.** §8.2 carries `GET /api/plans` and
         `GET`+`PUT /api/plans/:board`, resolving against the **server's** cwd and
         returning `409` outside a repository rather than writing into whatever directory
         happens to be current; §9.2 carries a **config editor** screen that includes
         boards. **The reasoning that settled it: a route follows the file**, and §12 puts
         the file at `<repo>/.dacode/plans/<board>.md`. So the "nearest existing concept is
         §6's **projects**" reading survives — but as **presentation** (§9.2 groups boards,
         and a board is cross-session by nature so it is not a tab of the session view)
         rather than as a second routing axis. Nothing had to be decided about projects
         after all, which is why this closed instead of needing a vote.
      2. ~~**No write path.**~~ → **`.dacode/plans/` is the third of §8.5's three writable
         classes**, beside user config and repo config, exactly as caveat #1 required.
         ⚠️ **What neither the caveat nor this item anticipated is that the allowlist also
         has to refuse *keys*, not only paths**: §8.5 rejects the exec-bearing parts of a
         writable file (`[[extensions]]`' `cmd`, a hook's `run`/`post`) because §9.2 renders
         model-authored markdown on the authenticated origin, so a script reaching that
         origin could otherwise turn one transcript into persistent command execution as the
         server's user. Boards are markdown and unaffected, but the rule lives in the same
         list they do. **And a board save is conditional**: `If-Match` on the `ETag` it read,
         `412` on mismatch — because §4.8's promotion writes the same file a UI saves, and
         "a human reviews the diff" is not a reconciliation mechanism for a clobber (the diff
         shows the result, not the bytes that were overwritten).
      3. ~~**`promote` needs a controller answer.**~~ → **Answered as two checks that do
         not substitute for each other.** The act is session-scoped (the item belongs to one
         session's tree) while its effect is not (a committed repo file), so §8.4 gates it
         on the **controller of the session owning the item** *and* §8.5/§8.2 bound the
         write. **The asymmetry this item did not state:** from the model a promotion is a
         **write through §4.4** (§4.8's own `Verify::Command` rule is the precedent — the
         task subsystem does not get to touch the filesystem outside the permission engine),
         while from a browser it is **not a tool call at all**, so §4.4 is not in the path
         and the allowlist is the bound instead. Neither door inherits the other's check.
      ⚠️ **What A7 recorded rather than fixed, and which gap 3 depends on:** §3.3 has **no
      task-mutation `Command`**, so the browser path to `promote` does not exist in the
      protocol yet — **U103**. This item is closed because the *design* questions it raised
      are answered; U103 is the wire gap underneath them and stays open with the task-tree
      brainstorm as owner.
- [x] **U57 · B16 must be read with B10 or it settles B10 by accident — DISSOLVED,
      not resolved.** The warning was well-founded: signing B16 as drafted *would*
      have settled B10 by accident. It was discharged by **narrowing the policy
      instead of by deciding both** — nothing ports to Rust, so no YAML crate can
      enter the tree and the choice the coupling existed to force cannot arise.
      **B10 is now free-standing** and can be signed on its own merits whenever.
      Two facts closed the other half: `agents-sync.py` *writes* YAML as well as
      parsing it, because the generated `.opencode/agent/*.md` frontmatter is
      **opencode's** format and not ours to choose; and Python has **no stdlib TOML
      writer** (`tomllib` is read-only, verified on 3.14.3), so moving the tracker
      would trade PyYAML for `tomlkit` — a lateral swap in a tool already slated for
      retirement. **PyYAML is permanent**, which is also why `agent-rules.yaml` does
      not convert early.
      *Original entry, kept because the audit trail is the rule:* three of the five
      Python tools parse YAML, so porting them either adds a YAML crate (`serde_yaml`
      is deprecated upstream and no YAML crate is in
      [Appendix F](appendices/F-c-dependencies.md)) or moves `agent-rules.yaml` and
      the tracker to TOML — which is B10's subject and would reuse `toml_edit`,
      already in Appendix F's clean list and already required by §5.1. **Every clause
      of that is now moot except the `toml_edit` fact**, which survives as the reason
      a TOML config would be cheap if one were ever wanted.
- [x] **U58 · Two of the five Python tools are prototypes of §4.8, so they should be
      retired, not ported — CONFIRMED, with both line counts stale.** `tasks.py`
      (~~261~~ **298** lines) *is* the task tree; `attention.py` (~~642~~ **860**) is
      a view over it. Porting either builds a second implementation of a spec'd
      product feature, and under §2.4 neither is ported: both stay Python and are
      **deleted** when their trigger fires. ~~**Retiring `tasks.py` is still blocked on
      §16.6**~~ ✅ **that blocker is discharged 2026-09-18**: §4.8 now carries
      `Standing` — goals only, exempt from a red `check` and from reminders — so the
      defect found in `tasks.py` is fixed in the product spec and would not be
      inherited. What remains before retirement is the M2 dogfooding trigger, not a
      design gap. The repo-side half is fixed (`--status standing`, 2026-09-14), which
      was *evidence for* §16.6 and is now also the shape §4.8 adopted. `attention.py`'s
      §4.8-view half dogfoods; its appendix/§6-scraping half has no product analogue
      and never will, so it is permanent.
- [x] **U59 · `check-links.py` may be the one tool that should stay Python
      permanently — IT DOES, and it won by default rather than on its own argument.**
      Decided before M0 as this item asked. Under §2.4 *every* authoring tool stays
      a script, so `check-links.py` is not a special case any more; its reasoning is
      nonetheless preserved in §2.4 as **the one genuine exception class** — tooling
      that must run on a checkout that has not been built — because it holds
      independently of how B16 came out. If link checking needed a compiled
      workspace, the docs could not be validated until the code builds, which
      inverts the order the design phase depends on. This item is also why §2.4's
      final paragraph existed as a proposal; it landed as the scope boundary instead.
- [x] **U60 · `attention.py` shipped a false-positive priority and an edit silently
      deleted a function — both caught only by running it.** The milestone
      heuristic matched a bare `M1` in prose ("M0 is still the right next step")
      and then, after tightening, still matched `all gate M1)` at the end of a
      74-character parenthetical, promoting an item to P0 on a sentence about
      *other* items; fixed by requiring a short bracketed tag or a gating
      preposition. Separately, an edit whose match was a single `def` line replaced
      the signature and orphaned the body after a `return`, so
      `earliest_milestone` was called but never defined — **`ast.parse` passed**,
      because Python cannot see a `NameError` at parse time and dead code after
      `return` is legal. **A syntax check is not a smoke test.** Recorded as f33's
      companion lesson: run the tool and check its output against known ground
      truth, every time.

### From the third-party review pass (session 8)

Three asks in one: *"an opinion on the current state of the design as a
third-party reviewer"*, *"good ideas from alibaba/open-code-review to incorporate
into the reviewer built-in agent"*, and *"a section/tasks about harness
benchmarking"*. They produced three new artefacts and one list:

| Ask | Produced |
|---|---|
| The reviewer ideas | the **fifth reference survey** ([open-code-review](../../.agents/knowledge/reference-harnesses/open-code-review.md) — a *specialist*, not a general harness) and decision **[B17](appendices/B-decisions.md)** |
| Harness benchmarking | decision **[B18](appendices/B-decisions.md)**, delta **[A21](appendices/A-design-deltas.md)** (§14 → §14.1/§14.2), and new doc **[33](part6-quality/33-benchmarking.md)** |
| The design review | the unchecked items below |

The review narrative itself went to the user; what is recorded here is only what
is **actionable and was not already tracked**. Nothing below is a taste objection
— each one is a place where the spec says something that is not true, or does not
say something it needs to.

**Method note, because it matters for how much weight these carry:** every item
was checked against `docs/dacode-design.md` as it stands at v0.1 / 2026-09-13, by
reading the cited sections rather than by recalling them. Where a claim depends on
who controls a value (which is most of the security group), the control path is
named explicitly instead of assumed — the A19 lesson that *a dependency claim is a
claim, not a fact*.

#### Security seams — the group worth reading first

- [x] **U61 · ⚠️ §7.1 hooks are a template-into-shell seam, and it is the same class of
      defect as the `Verify::Command` one that was caught for §4.8.** `run` gets
      "the envelope on stdin **and templated args**", with the example
      `notify-send 'dacode' '{{ session.title }}: {{ reason }}'` — a *string*
      interpolated into a shell command. The example's own fields are
      client-controlled rather than model-controlled, so state the risk precisely:
      the **mechanism is general**, hooks fire on `QuestionAsked` and
      `PermissionRequested` (§7.1's second example does exactly this), and the
      natural fields to interpolate there — the question `prompt`, a tool name, an
      error message — are **model-authored**. A hook author writing
      `{{ prompt }}` has written a command-injection bug and the spec gives them no
      reason not to. **Fix: argv, not a shell string; no interpolation into the
      command at all.** The envelope is already on stdin, which is the complete
       mechanism — so *delete* templated args rather than escape them.
       ~~Separately, `post` ships the **whole `Envelope`** to an arbitrary URL with no
       redaction rule, while §8.2 redacts secrets on `/api/config`; that asymmetry
       should be closed or explained.~~ ✅ **The second half is closed — B19/A23,
       2026-09-16.** §7.1 now requires a `post` body to be redacted before it leaves
       and says why the local `run` path is *not*; §8.2 names the four projection
       endpoints plus `/api/config` as the redaction points. Cite §7.1/§8.2 rather
       than restating the argument. **The first half stands and is still A22 item 1.**
       Belongs in [24](part5-outreach/24-extensions-channels.md)
       **Now delta A22, item 1.** Owed by M4 — but the delta itself can land any
       time, and should, because it is three lines of spec text. ✅ **A22 signed 2026-09-17
       with item 1 confirmed — amended in one particular:** `run` takes an argv array with no
       shell, and **templating survives into argv elements** rather than being deleted, since
       with no shell there is nothing to inject into and the convenience is free. A hook that
       genuinely wants `sh -c` must ask for it explicitly, which is the point of making it
       visible.
      ✅ **CLOSED 2026-09-18 by A22 item 1, in exactly the amended form recorded above.**
      §7.1's `run` is now an **argv array executed without a shell**, with templating
      surviving **into argv elements** — so `{{ session.title }}` expands to one argument
      whatever it contains, and a title holding `; rm -rf ~` is an argument rather than a
      second command. A hook that genuinely wants a shell must write `["sh","-c",…]`, which
      is the point: the dangerous case becomes visible in the config file where a reviewer
      can see it, instead of being the default behaviour of every hook that interpolates a
      field. `when` keeps its expression language because an expression is *evaluated* and
      never executed. **§7.1 also states why this is a rule and not an example-level
      detail**, which is the part this item argued for and the spec previously lacked: the
      example's own fields are client-controlled, but the natural fields to interpolate on
      `QuestionAsked`/`PermissionRequested` — the prompt, a tool name, an error message — are
      **model-authored**, so `"{{ prompt }}"` in a shell string is a model-reachable
      command-injection bug and nothing about the field name warns the author. §14 has the
      test (fire a hook whose template expands to `; rm -rf ~`, assert one argv element and
      no second process). **Note the fix kept the convenience this item proposed deleting**:
      deleting templating would have been safer and less useful, and the argv form makes
      both available at once, which is the only combination worth having.
- [x] **U62 · ⚠️ `AllowPattern` lets an extension widen permissions without limit, and
      §8.4 grants extensions that power on purpose — ✅ FIXED 2026-09-18, not merely
      documented.** §3.3's
      `ResolvePermission { decision: AllowPattern(String) }` injects a caller-chosen
      glob; §4.4 puts session grants at the **top** of the resolution order, above
      agent, project and user config; §8.4 says extensions may answer
      permissions *"regardless of control"* because that is their purpose. Compose
      the three and a Telegram bridge answering one prompt can grant `**` for the
      session — i.e. any connected bridge is effectively root-equivalent, which is
      not what §8.3's "no users, no roles" model intends. **Two separable fixes:**
      constrain `AllowPattern` to a **subset of the scope actually requested** (the
      request is in `PermissionRequested`, so this is checkable), and split the
      `Hello` capability so *answer questions* and *grant permissions* are
      different flags. Belongs in [16](part3-capabilities/16-permissions.md) and
      [24](part5-outreach/24-extensions-channels.md). **Now delta A22, item 2.** The
      `AllowPattern` half is owed by M1 (the permission engine); the capability split by M4.
      ⚠️ **Both halves changed owner on 2026-09-17.** A22's item 2 was **redirected to
      permissive for v1**, so the split does not arrive from there; and **B20's resolution
      needs it for remote principals specifically**, which is now **A25's §8.4 half** —
      argued on its own merits (a process on another machine is not a local bridge), with

#### Correctness gaps

- [x] **U66 · The append-only event log has no version record — ✅ CLOSED 2026-09-18,
      folded into A1's transcription, which is where this item said it belonged.**
      The cheap answer was taken: line 1 of `events.jsonl` is now a **`LogHeader`**
      record — `{"type":"LogHeader","data":{"format_version":1,"created":<unix millis>}}`
      — and **not** an `Envelope`, so it carries no cursor and needs no tier. It is
      written once at creation and never rewritten, so it costs the append-only
      property nothing. Two details worth keeping: `format_version` is **the same
      counter §7.2's `Hello` sends**, so a log and a wire version cannot drift apart;
      and §12's layout text records that the header has no index entry, the first
      `index.bin` record being the first event. ⚠️ **It reworded a sentence A24 had
      landed the day before** — the cursor's "equals line number + 1" became
      "derivable by arithmetic from the record's position", because a header on line 1
      shifts any position-derived arithmetic. That *strengthens* U67's fix rather than
      undoing it: a fixed `+1` was exactly the weld to the JSONL representation U67
      was closed to remove. Original entry follows. §14 pins the wire format
      with golden fixtures and §7.2 sends `Hello { protocol_version }` to
      extensions — but nothing stamps a version into `events.jsonl` itself. A log
      written by one build and read by a later one has no way to know what it is
      looking at, which is a strange gap in the one artefact the design calls the
      source of truth. A header record at log head is the cheap answer; a field on
      `Envelope` is the expensive one. **A1 is the natural place**, since it is
      already re-shaping `Envelope`/`Event`, and it is *cheaper before the first
      fixture exists* than after. **Owed by M1**, and in practice by A1.

      branch rather than the answer.** What landed is a retryable overflow with **two
      branches** — compact-and-re-issue when compaction is enabled, otherwise terminate
      through §4.2's guard set **with a remedy the user can act on** (`/compact`, a
      hand-over, a fork) — stated in §6 as a provider-level path and in §4.5 as the
      estimate's consequence, with §6 recording why overflow is *not* a 429 (backing off
      and retrying the same request cannot succeed; the request itself is too large).
      **The composition is the finding:** amendment (a) defers compaction, A3 landed the
      hand-over as a *slot* not a mechanism, and this item's fix assumed compaction — so
      v1 had no automatic response to a filling context and both candidates were
      unavailable. Closing U68 therefore forced v1's honest default into the spec:

- [x] **U71 · `cost_usd: Option<f64>` will be wrong, not merely imprecise, until A4
      lands — ✅ DONE 2026-09-18, via A4, taking the first of the two options this item
      offered.** With prompt caching a turn has four rates — input, cache-write,
      cache-read, output — and §3.2's `Usage` had no cache fields, so any cost computed
      silently priced cached reads at full input rate. **A wrong cost number is worse
      than an absent one**, because it will be believed. ~~Either A4 first, or `cost_usd`
      stays `None` until it lands.~~ **A4 landed, and `Usage` is now a real struct with
      all four counters** — which it had to become anyway, since `TurnFinished` and
      `SubAgentFinished` had both been naming a type that existed nowhere in the spec
      (the fourth instance of that class in two days; see the tracker's `f77`/`f79`).
      §6 now states that cost is computed from **four rates matched to those four
      counters**, with the argument for putting them on the *event* rather than leaving
      them a §6 computation detail: a cached read priced at the input rate overstates
      exactly the saving the cache exists to deliver. A provider reporting no cache
      counters yields zeros, and a zero is honest — it says nothing was cached, which for
      such a provider is true. **A second consequence this item did not predict:** the
      four counters are what make the cache hit rate *measurable rather than inferred*,
      which is what §14.2's benchmarking tier and **B18's T2** both need — so T2 gained
      its input fields as a side effect of a cost-accuracy fix. (Floats for money is a
      lesser, separate quibble, and **stays open as such** — it is not part of this item
      and A4 did not address it.) **Owed by M1** — discharged in the spec.

#### Wording that is doing more work than it can carry

- [ ] **U72 · The "no cross-session memory" non-goal is now load-bearing and imprecise.**
      §4.8's promoted `.dacode/plans/` boards, §5.6's `AGENTS.md` assembly and §12's
      `index.json` are all cross-session state, and §4.8 already has to argue its
      way out of the contradiction. The actual rule the design follows is better and
      should simply be stated: **nothing accumulates without a human-reviewed
      diff.** "No memory" is the slogan; that is the principle. A12 (the §16/§1
      bookkeeping pass) is the right place.
- [ ] **U73 · §5.4's six-line workflow example uses two different addressing schemes** —
      `{{ steps.plan.result }}` and `{{ steps[2].result }}` — which is cosmetic on
      its own but is a symptom of the already-tracked "pick the templating approach"
      follow-up. Whichever template language is chosen, the example should use one
      form.

      genuinely unusual (retracted benchmark figures, a corrected delta dependency,
      a defect patched back into the artefact rather than only logged). But every
      decision so far has been made against surveys and reasoning, never against a
      running system, and that is the one input the process cannot supply to itself.
      **Concrete recommendation: batch-sign the four high-confidence M1 blockers
      (B3, B5, B7, B14 — all `accept`-recommended at high confidence) in one pass
      and scaffold M0 now.** M0 is gated on nothing. Its value is not the code; it
      is that "verification is design consistency" becomes "does it compile".
      (This overlaps the existing "worth deciding whether to batch the votes" item

      other direction.)

      line naming a decision that does not exist is reported rather than silently

      were negative-tested (deliberately broken, confirmed to fail, restored), not
      just run green. **This is the "machine-readable front matter" fix that the
      entry below argued for four times — done for the one field that kept
      misfiring, not for the whole table.** The original finding follows, kept as
      the audit trail.
      *Original:* **the backtick escape did not protect the action matcher,
      and this pass reproduced the bug to find out.** Writing B18 mislabelled it
      `measure` on the first run, because `action_for_decision` scans a decision's
      **detail section** for the phrases B12 uses to mark itself — and B18's detail
      necessarily *quotes* B12 while explaining that it unblocks it. This is the
      f19/f20/f33 class again ("writing about a machine-readable form makes you an
      instance of it"), but with a new wrinkle: the documented escape is inline
      code, and **this matcher strips `` ` `` before matching** (a deliberate fix,
      because B12's own signal is emphasised). So backticking is *not* an escape
      here. Worked around by rewording B18 to avoid the literal phrases, with a
      note in its detail saying why. **The durable fix is the one already named
      for the appendix tables: machine-readable front matter instead of scraping
      prose** — an `action: vote` field cannot be triggered by a quotation. Same
      run, a second instance of the same class: putting *"unblocks B12"* in the
      **Gates** column made `norm_docs` read `B12` as plan-doc **12** — the
      checkpoints doc — and derive its milestone from that. **Rule: the Gates cell
      takes doc numbers only; B-numbers belong in prose.** Both were caught by
      checking the tool's output against known ground truth, not by its exit code
      — f35's lesson, third confirmation. **And then this very entry became a
      fourth**: its first draft named that doc's milestone inside a short
      parenthetical, which is precisely the shape f35 taught the milestone
      heuristic to match, so an item gating nothing was promoted to P1. Four
      instances across three different matchers is no longer a run of bad luck —
      it is the argument for machine-readable front matter, made four times.
- [x] **U76 · §6 has grown into a ~600-line append-only stream with no item ids —
      DONE**, which was the same failure mode §16.6 and §4.8's gate are about: a
      list that is always long gets skimmed, and then a real finding is invisible
      inside it — exactly how §16.6 was lost. `attention.py` was the right first
      response; stable ids were the next, and every item below now carries one
      (`U1`–`U79`), so an item can be *cited and closed* rather than restated.
      The cost this entry predicted was real and is handled: an id is another
      mechanically-read form, so **it sits inside the leading bold run, after the
      checkbox**, and flipping `[ ]` to `[x]` cannot change it. `attention.py`
      reads the id instead of the line number it used to synthesise — line numbers
      move on every edit, which is why citing `§6:1071` was already useless by the
      next session. Two hygiene checks guard it: ids must be **unique across closed
      items too** (a reused number silently re-points an old citation), and every
      item must have one. Both negative-tested. **Never renumber**: a new item takes
      the next unused number wherever it sits, so gaps are expected and meaningful.

      substance the substance wins — recorded rather than silently encoded.

      93, which is the evidence that rows moved rather than vanished; the delivered
      tree reports **90 open items at 36 P0**, because this pass also closed four
      (U30, U31, U50, U76) and opened one (U79).
      **Two hygiene checks guard it, both negative-tested:** a `gates:` line naming
      an absent or already-applied delta is reported, and — the actual regression
      guard — **any open delta left with no milestone at all is reported**, which
      is the failure that was silent before. Broken three ways (unknown id,
      out-of-range milestone, removed declaration), confirmed to fail, restored.
      **Method note, because it is U53's lesson a sixth time:** this was found by

- [ ] **U79 · ⚠️ Raised in priority by B16: the tools are now *permanent*, and
      permanent untested code is worse than transitional untested code.** §2.4 says
      authoring tooling is not awaiting a port, so there is no future Rust rewrite
      that inherits `cargo test` for free — this is the only implementation these
      checks will ever have, and §14 now records the gap in the spec rather than
      leaving it implicit. *Original entry:* `tools/` has no test runner, so every check is verified by hand and
      the verification is not repeatable.** This pass added **eighteen** negative
      and edge-case probes across three tools — three ways to break the new
      `gates:` declarations, four cases for the no-link convention, two for the §6
      ids, six for the `standing` status, and three more that the review round
      forced (a reported line number, a run from another directory, a FAIL row whose
      detail contradicted it) — and every one was an inline shell one-off: mutate a
      tracked file, run, eyeball, restore. None of it is committed, so the next
      person who edits `attention.py` gets no regression signal at all, and the
      *only* reason the defects it finds are believed is that someone re-ran the
      experiment. **That dual review then found six defects in the new code and five
      doc claims that did not reproduce — after all eighteen probes had passed — is
      the argument for a runner, and for review, in one sentence.**
      Two concrete costs already paid, both now in `.agents/pitfalls-live.md`:
      **P-LIVE-001** (`$?` after a pipe reports the last command, which twice
      reported a failing gate as passing) and **P-LIVE-002** (`set -e` aborted a
      negative-test script before its restore step, leaving a deliberately-corrupted
      tracked file on disk). Both are symptoms of asserting on exit codes in shell
      rather than in a harness.
      The evidence that this matters is the bug record itself: **U53** lists four
      `attention.py` defects, **U75** a fifth, **U78** a sixth — all found by
      running the tool against ground truth, none by a test, and each one a
      *silently wrong* table rather than a crash. A doc-scraping tool fails by
      looking plausible.
      **Shape it should take, and the constraint that decides the language:** these
      tools must stay runnable **before the workspace builds**, or the docs cannot be
      validated during the design phase — which is the same argument **U59** makes
      for `check-links.py` staying Python permanently. So a Python test runner over
      `tools/` (fixtures + expected table rows + expected exit codes), not Rust
      `xtask` tests. Interacts with **B16/A20**: if the tools move to `xtask`, the
      runner moves with them, and `tasks.py`/`attention.py` are the two B16 says to
      *retire and dogfood* rather than port. Cheap enough to do now, and it pays for
      itself the first time a regex is edited.
      **This entry is its own seventh data point, and it happened while writing it.**
      The first draft placed a milestone tag after a gating preposition, and
      `milestone_in_prose` matched the construction, promoting an item that gates no
      milestone to **P0**. U75 records the same thing happening to itself; U53
      records it happening four times before that. Reworded rather than left wrong —
      but note what rewording means: **prose is being written to satisfy a regex**,
      which is the scraper's cost made visible.
      **Describing the trigger reproduces it, and here the backtick escape does not
      help.** Quoting the offending two words in the paragraph that reports them
      re-armed the matcher — twice, because the correction quoted them again. That is
      the U30/f19 rule a third time: describing a machine-readable form makes the
      description an instance of it. Unlike `check-links.py` and the depth grep,
      `milestone_in_prose` receives text with only `**` stripped — **inline code is
      not removed before matching** — so backticking a milestone construction is
      *not* an escape in this tool. U30's claim that backticking is "the supported
      escape" holds for the two matchers it names and not for this one.
      The durable fix is the one U53 names: §6 items declare a milestone the way
      Appendix A's deltas now do, instead of having one inferred from a sentence —
      and until then, a §6 entry that names a milestone must expect to be ranked by
      it.

in the crate tree), §2.2 (**no crate depends on `xtask`**) and §14. The resolution
is **narrower than the recommendation**, and the narrowing is the substance: the
user's rule was that repo/docs tooling which neither ships nor is required by the
harness may stay Python, and applied to all five tools that leaves nothing to port.
So §2.4 is **two classes with a scope boundary**, not a Rust default with
exceptions pending deletion. B10's coupling dissolved as a result (U57), the
`check-links.py` dissent won by default (U59), and both dispositions were confirmed
(U58). The full dossier correction — including the three claims the recommendation
got wrong — is in [Appendix B](appendices/B-decisions.md) under B16's banner.

- [ ] **U89 · The sandbox/`yolo` indicator is colour-only, and colour is a fragile
      channel for a *security* state.** Settled by the user with U86: *"in TUI mode
      we can inform the modes (sandbox/yolo) in colors, not necessary to have
      explicit name it."* Recorded as a decision, not relitigated — but B7's whole
      subject is honesty about what is actually enforced, and a state that is
      encoded only in colour is a state that can be present and unseen. Four
      concrete cases: a **monochrome or low-colour terminal** (and `TERM=dumb`,
      which a `run -p` pipeline may well set), a **colour-blind user**, a
      **screenshot or pasted transcript** — which is how a session gets discussed
      after the fact, and the one place the state would most need to survive — and
      the **web UI** (§9.2, mobile-first), where the TUI's palette does not
      automatically carry over.
      **Cheapest mitigations, none of which adds a printed label to the status
      line:** colour plus a distinct **glyph** (so the two states differ in shape as
      well as hue), and the explicit name available **on demand** — `/status`, or a
      hover/tooltip in the web UI — so it is checkable without being permanent
      screen furniture. A third option is to name it only at the **transition**,
      i.e. when `SetPermMode` moves a session into `yolo`, which is the moment the
      user is looking.
      **Recommended variant, the cheapest that survives all four cases: colour *plus*
      one distinct glyph** (`⚡` yolo, `▣` sandboxed — a single cell, so the state
      survives monochrome, colour-blindness and a screenshot), the explicit name on
      `/status` and as a web-UI tooltip, and a one-line announcement **at the
      transition** into `yolo`, which is the moment attention is already on the status
      line. Colours come from the theme, with a defined fallback for themes that omit
      them.
      Belongs in [22-tui](part4-hosts-clients/22-tui.md) and
      [21-web-ui](part4-hosts-clients/21-web-ui.md) when each is deepened, and the
      glyph half is cheap enough to decide now. **Interaction:** U19 already asks for
      doc 22 to be deepened with theme auto-detect *before first paint*; a
      security-state colour belongs in that same theme work rather than being
      hardcoded, and both must survive a theme that does not define it.

- [ ] **U90 · Opt-in injection of live usage and context statistics back into the
      prompt — a new feature requested with B20's Q8 answer, and it has one hard
      constraint that decides its mechanism.** The ask: *"to have an option where
      harness could inject current usage/context back as a prompt (i.e. live
      statistics/hints for the model). opt-in feature."* Sound idea with real
      precedent — oh-my-pi injects goal-mode counters per turn and forge pushes a
      `system_reminder` on its End lifecycle (f23, f25) — and ⚠️ **per-turn numbers
      are exactly the volatile data §13.4 forbids in the cached prefix**: "anything
      volatile — timestamps, per-request ids, tool ordering — stays out of it". A token
      count that changes every turn, written into the stable prefix, would destroy the
      prompt cache on every turn — the very thing B18's headline metric measures.
      **So the mechanism is decided by the constraint rather than by taste:** it rides
      in an **appended, droppable B14 segment** (or a `system_reminder`-shaped
      message), never in the prefix. f25 is precedent for the exclusion as well as the
      injection — oh-my-pi *deliberately* keeps its volatile counters out of reviewer
      and export context because they change every turn. **Two second-order questions
      for whoever builds it:** a model that can see its own budget changes behaviour
      (which is the point), but the hint then becomes prompt surface that B18's T2
      overhead number must count; and §4.5's compaction threshold interacts with a hint
      that says "you are at 78 %".
      **Recommended mechanism:** a `system_reminder`-shaped message appended per turn
      behind `[context] usage_hints = true`, carrying **counters only** — context %
      used, session tokens, cost so far, turns used / `max_turns`, and §4.8's gate
      state, which is rendered anyway. **No timestamp**, because §13.4 names timestamps
      as the volatile case; counters change too, but they sit *outside* the prefix so
      nothing is invalidated. Being appended and droppable, compaction can drop it and
      lose nothing, and f25's exclusion rule applies: it stays out of exported and
      reviewer context. Belongs in
      [09](part2-engine/09-context-caching.md) and [10](part2-engine/10-compaction.md),
      and needs B14's segment index to exist first.

      they bypass a gate. The user asked to drop "explicitly asked" for *commits*
      — this is the narrower reading, flagged at the time rather than assumed.

- [x] **U93 · A refused lock has no exit status, and "session already held" is an
      operational state rather than a failure.** Surfaced by applying A24, not by
      reading for it. §3.6 now guarantees a second opener **fails fast with the holder
      named and `attach` offered** — but §11 documents exit codes *only* for `run`
      (`0 done, 2 needs input, 3 blocked on permission, 1 error`), and B21's sub-answer
      5 says the commands that actually hit the lock are **`session fork` and resume**,
      neither of which has any documented exit code. So a refusal falls through to a
      generic `1`, indistinguishable from a crash.
      **Why that is worth a code of its own.** `run` already got **3** for exactly this
      shape of case: "blocked on permission" is not an error, it is a state a caller
      must branch on, and CI cannot tell it from a bug without a distinct status. A held
      session is the same thing — *retryable, somebody else's fault, and the remedy is
      known* (`attach`, or wait). A script that forks sessions in a loop would otherwise
      have to parse stderr to learn whether to retry.
      **Not invented here.** Assigning a number is a small design decision and §11 has
      no slot for it; the honest fix is to extend §11's exit-code table to the other
      subcommands and give a held session its own value in the same edit, rather than
      bolting a code onto a section that documents one command. **Owed by M1**, when the
      CLI is built and doc [23](part4-hosts-clients/23-cli.md) is deepened — and it is
      cheap to settle then because nothing has shipped to stay compatible with.
      Related and also undocumented: what `session fork` should do when the *parent* is
      held, since forking a live session is the case B21's sub-answer 5 names first.
      ⚠️ **Corrected 2026-09-19 — this is not a gap M1 can cheaply fill, and the item
      cites the decision it would overturn without noticing.** B21's sub-answer 5 is
      quoted above for *which* commands hit the lock, but not for *what it decided*:
      "Both: error plus `attach`." Under §11's mapping `Error` → 1, so the "generic `1`"
      this item calls indistinguishable from a crash is the **signed** outcome rather than
      an omission — and giving a held session its own code therefore *overturns B21*,
      which is the user's decision and not an M1 detail. **A second consequence, also
      unstated here:** §11's four codes are "a mapping from `IdleReason`, not a separate
      vocabulary," and a refused lock cannot be an `IdleReason` at all, because that enum
      says why an *agent loop* went idle (`AgentIdle { reason, guard }`) while a refused
      lock means no loop was ever entered **in this process** — on `session fork` no child
      exists yet, and on resume the session is on disk but held elsewhere, so in neither
      case is there an idle loop to report a reason for. So the code cannot be added to the
      existing mapping; §11 would have to grow a second vocabulary for pre-session failures,
      ending the property that the exit-code space has one source of truth. That is a design
      change, not the "small design decision" this item calls it. Still owed by M1 and
      still cheap *relative to post-ship*, but it needs the user first — and doc 23 still
      carries its depth marker, so nothing here may be deepened yet (hard rule 1).

### From the 2026-09-17 decision pass (session 14)

Twelve B-decisions, fifteen deltas and design §16 item 6 were signed in one pass; §1's
banner carries the amendments and §3 is now the application queue. Three things that pass
created are nobody's to guess at, so they are items rather than footnotes:

      `parse_spec_16` lists every numbered item in §16 and has no notion of a resolved one;
      only A12's §16 pass removes it. The one view that exists to catch "recorded in the
      spec but absent from Appendix B" — which is how §16.6 went missing in the first place
      — now **under-reports owed work by fifteen items and over-reports open votes by
      one**. Same missing state, two symptoms. **Interim, stated so nobody is misled:**
      §3 above is the application queue and the only carrier of it, and §16.6's P0 row is a
      known false positive until A12 lands. *2026-09-18: the false positive is now
      doubly false — §16.6's answer (`Standing`) is normative in §4.8, so the P0 vote
      the tool renders is not merely decided but **applied**, and A12's job is only the

      edit §16 piecemeal, on the reasoning that §16 is a list of open decisions and

      `approved:` marker in Appendix A's `attention-meta` block rendering as `do: apply`,

      🔧 **HALF FIXED 2026-09-18 — the §16 half, not the delta half.** The second clause of
      that fix is built: `parse_spec_16` now classifies from each item's **own text**
      (a `✅`/`~~` marker resolves it, a `B<n>` reference makes it Appendix B's, only an

      **M1.9 and M1.10** in §5's sub-step table (2026-09-19), which is why the hand-over

- [ ] **U97 · Partial compaction is a candidate, not a feature, and it fights the cache.**
      A4's second amendment, in the user's words: *"it could be partial compaction (by
      stripping some later tools output that doesn't affect the following conversation, but
      requires some experiments while could affect caching)"*. Two hazards are why it stays
      a candidate: stripping earlier tool output **rewrites bytes already sent**, which §4.8
      forbids for context rendering and which A4's own append-only rule exists to prevent —
      so it must go through the truncate-and-re-emit resync path, never a byte-rewrite — and
      it **destroys the prompt-cache prefix from the cut point onwards**, trading a cache
      miss for context space. Whether that trade pays is precisely what **B18's T2
      cache-hit-rate metric** measures, and B18 was signed the same day, so the instrument
      exists. **Owner: A4's application plus B18-T2. Do not adopt before the number** — that
      is B18's publication rule applied to a design choice rather than to a claim.
      ⚠️ **Still open after A4 applied 2026-09-18, which is the correct outcome and not a
      miss.** A4's half of the ownership is **discharged**: §4.5 now records partial
      compaction as a **candidate, not an adopted feature**, with both hazards named in
      the spec rather than only here — it rewrites bytes already sent, so it must go
      through the truncate-and-re-emit resync path and never a byte-rewrite; and it
      destroys the cache prefix from the cut point onwards, trading a cache miss for
      context space, a trade §14.2's hit-rate metric is the instrument for. What remains
      is **B18-T2's half, which is a measurement and cannot be discharged by prose**: the
      number does not exist, so the feature is not adopted. Two things changed its
      prospects while it was open. ~~**§14.2 does not exist yet** — A21 is signed but

      rather than by content, and **A21 must place it**.~~ ✅ **A21 applied 2026-09-18 and
      §14.2 exists, and it names this gate explicitly**: partial compaction "is recorded
      there as a candidate rather than a feature because it trades a cache miss for context

      **`Usage` now carries the four
      counters** (A4, closing U71), so T2 has the cache-read and cache-write inputs a hit

- [ ] **U98 · The sandbox seam has a named v2 route, supplied by the user at B7's
      sign-off: intercept `execve` through a BPF filter.** *"For sandbox variant, we can
      intercept execve via bpf filters and there we can capture exact program path and,
      optionally, parameters. Similar to `sandboxed-api` built on top of `sandbox2`"*
      (both Google; github.com/google/sandboxed-api,
      developers.google.com/code-sandboxing/sandbox2). **Why this is more than an
      implementation note: it answers B7's own central argument instead of working around
      it.** A glob over a command *string* cannot decide what the command does — that is
      why §4.4's allow-list and `bash:readonly` are advisory, and why U12/U63 exist. The
      kernel at `execve` sees the **resolved binary path and its argv**, so `git diff; git
      push`, `bash -c …`, a shell function, an alias and a symlink all stop being evasions.
      It is therefore the mechanism that makes read-onlyness **enforced** rather than
      documented — i.e. it *retires* the honesty fix — and it is what **B20**'s remote
      members actually need, since B7's stub means its "sandboxed or refused" rule has
      nothing to point at today.
      **Two costs to settle before it is anything but a lead.** *(a)* **Dependency policy:**
      Rust BPF loaders are `aya` (pure-Rust loader) and `libbpf-rs` (links `libbpf`), and the
      filter itself is compiled at build time — which is §2.3/§2.4 territory and a *different*
      question from linking C at runtime, but needs an answer and possibly an Appendix F row.
      *(b)* **`sandboxed-api` and `sandbox2` are C++**, so they are the source of the
      technique and not a candidate dependency — **the lead is the mechanism, not the
      library.** Also worth noting: BPF-based interception is Linux-specific, so a macOS
      arm of the same seam wants `sandbox-exec`/Seatbelt or Endpoint Security, and the
      `SandboxBackend` seam B7 reserves is exactly the place that per-OS split belongs.
      ⚠️ **2026-10-01, and this item gains a *predecessor* obligation rather than a new one: the user made
      the permission matcher adoptable by this route a condition of ruling g128.** Ruling arm 5
      (hand-rolled, `Domain`-parameterised, +0 packages) came with *"the pattern should be adoptable for
      our strict sandbox as well (similar to google's sandbox2/sandboxed-api, where we can filter on linux
      syscalls via ebpf)"* — i.e. **this item's mechanism is now a design constraint on M1.7's matcher, not
      only a v2 lead.** Four consequences are written into doc 16 §16.5 so M1.7 builds to them rather than
      discovering them: the matcher is a **pure predicate over `(Domain, pattern, subject bytes)`** with no
      `PermScope` in its signature, so a sandbox evaluator can call it with a path lifted out of a syscall
      argument; ⚠️ **`Domain`'s variants must not be named for §4.4's config keys** (`Path`, not `Edit`) —
      a sandbox filter needs the same *matching* semantics over subjects no TOML key names, and renaming
      after M1.3 publishes is a wire-adjacent change; the pattern language must be able to name a
      syscall-level subject, which is this item's own argument (at `execve` the kernel sees the resolved
      path and argv, so §16.10's evasions stop being evasions); and ⚠️ **"adoptable" cannot mean the glob
      runs in the filter** — a seccomp-BPF program executes in the kernel over raw register values and
      cannot call a userspace matcher, so adoptable means the *vocabulary* is shared and the matcher is
      callable from the **userspace half** of a notify-based filter (seccomp user notification, or an eBPF
      LSM hook). Anything arguing otherwise is arguing about a different mechanism. **Verify (added):**
      whoever fills the stub finds a matcher it can reuse without a rename, and if it cannot, the reason is
      recorded here rather than worked around by a second matcher — two pattern languages in one product is
      the §16.4 defect one layer up.
      **Owner: whoever fills the stub — M5 at the earliest, and B20's design session should
      read this before it assumes container containment.**

### From applying A14 (session 16)

- [x] **U99 · ✅ CLOSED 2026-09-19 by A7 — both halves of the channel are normative, and
      the adjacent question this item queued was answered once as asked.** *A folder
      rename reaches no client but the one that issued it, and the fix is §8.2's, not the
      protocol's.* A14 made the organization registry authoritative
      for **names** (§12's `org.json`), because a name appears in no session log and so
      cannot be folded; membership, which *is* folded, converges on every client as
      principle 1 requires. Names do not. Every channel in §3.7 is per-session — an
      `Envelope` carries a `session`, `Subscribe` names one — so a rename has nowhere to
      travel, and its issuer learns it only from the `Ack`. §3.7's "never silently stale"
      promise is therefore **scoped to a session**, with the registry named as the one
      exception rather than left as a counterexample.
      **Why it is narrow rather than a hole.** A client reads the trees when it renders
      them, so visible staleness needs two clients holding a session list open at the
      same moment as a rename. Nothing is *lost*: the registry is authoritative and the
      next read is correct, which is different from §3.7's durable-event case where a
      missed envelope needs a resync.
      ~~**What closing it means, and why it is A7's, owed by M3.**~~ ✅ **Closed by A7
      2026-09-19, and the shape is exactly the one prescribed here**: a freshness
      channel — a registry version on the tree reads plus a hint on the socket — landed as
      HTTP-surface work at §8.2 rather than in the replay contract. **The read half** is
      `org_version` on all four tree reads (`GET /api/sessions?project=&tag=&folder=&q=`,
      `/api/projects`, `/api/tags`, `/api/folders`), backed by a monotonic `version` stored
      *in* `org.json` (§12) rather than derived from mtime, because mtime is not monotonic
      across a rename-on-write, a restore from backup, or two hosts sharing a home
      directory — and a freshness token that can go backwards silently makes a client that
      trusts it stale forever. **The socket half** is §3.6's **third down-frame kind,
      `Hint`**, and it is a *compatibility event*: additive, and deliberately **not** an
      `Envelope` — no `session`, no `seq`, no cursor, never written, never replayed, safe
      to lose, since the authoritative version travels on the read it prompts. It gets **no
      golden fixture**, because §14.1 derives the fixture set from `Event`'s variants, and
      §14.1's new bullet asserts the three properties instead.
      ~~**A7 should answer one adjacent question at the same time, once rather than three
      times: who may write a non-session resource from a browser.**~~ ✅ **Answered once,
      as asked**: §8.4 now states **one rule for every non-session write** — the registry,
      the config writes and a board write are the same act, *a client changed something
      durable outside any session* — so v1's "any authenticated principal" covers all three
      and tightening is one decision rather than three. ⚠️ **But the mechanism this item
      named was wrong, and correcting it is why the answer is stronger.** It said the rule
      should use "`Hello`'s reserved capability flags"; **`Hello` is not a `Command`** — it
      is §7.2's extension handshake — so a flag there cannot gate a *browser*, and a tenant
      cannot gate a *bridge*. §8.3 now names **two seams required to express one policy**:
      the `Authenticator` for browser principals, `Hello`'s flags for extensions. Same
      correction shape as U62's annotation under A22: the item's diagnosis was right and
      its prescription was written before the mechanism was checked.
      **Rejected, so it is not re-proposed later:** widening `Envelope.session` to make
      the registry an event stream. It would re-open §3.6's cursor, lock and fencing
      questions for a second stream whose contents are not append-only in the first
      place, and it would touch every envelope one day after A1 settled them.

### From applying A5 and A9 (session 16, capabilities and M1's last delta)

- [x] **U101 · §14 has no UI test tier at all, so two client rules are now normative
      with nothing that can fail on them — ✅ DONE 2026-09-18, via A21, exactly as this
      item assigned it.** **A21's split added a `Clients` bullet to §14.1 carrying both
      properties as tests** — mouse tracking off unless an overlay holds the alternate
      screen (assert the enable *and* disable sequences, and that neither appears
      otherwise), and collapse-on-paste honouring the 10-line / 1000-char boundary with a
      chip the cursor cannot enter. **The harness is deliberately not named, and that is
      the part of this item's own reasoning that survived contact with the fix**: the TUI
      crate does not exist and §9.1's framework decision is open, so §14.1 fixes the
      *properties* — which outlive any harness — and leaves the backend to M1. **The web
      UI's half stays open with it**, since §9.1 lands at M3; this item closes on the TUI
      properties it named and not on UI testing generally. Original entry follows.
      §14's layers are Protocol, Engine, Tools,
      Server, Session log, Storage codec, Prompt caching, Providers, Extensions,
      `xtask` and repository authoring tooling — **there is no TUI or web-UI tier**, and
      A9 just made two rules normative that live entirely in a client:
      - **Mouse tracking is enabled only while a fullscreen overlay holds the alt
        screen** (§10). The failure is not a crash, it is a user who has permanently
        lost scroll-back and text selection in their own terminal — the two things a
        terminal does better than any UI — and it is invisible to every existing test
        because nothing asserts on the escape sequences emitted.
      - **Collapse-on-paste above 10 lines / 1000 chars into an indivisible chip**
        (§10). The failure is a chip the cursor can enter and half-edit, which looks
        like text and is not, so the model receives something the user never saw. The
        thresholds are numbers, and numbers drift.
      **Why this was recorded instead of fixed:** adding a UI test tier means choosing a
      harness for a crate that does not exist yet (ratatui's `TestBackend` for the TUI,
      and something else entirely for the web UI once §9.1's framework decision lands at
      M3), which is a §14 restructuring of the kind **A21** does — and A21 is signed but
      unapplied. Inventing a tier inside a two-section delta would have pre-empted it.
      **Owner: A21's §14 split, or M1.1 if A21 lands first.** A21 should place these two
      as the tier's first content rather than leaving them as the only two normative
      client rules with no test. Related: **U19** still owes doc 22's deepening, whose
      source is now §10 rather than the survey.

      `rand_core`, `chacha20`, `cpufeatures`, `getrandom`, `libc`, `r-efi`) and adds
      back three (`serde` + its derive pair) — net four, 28 → 24. **Consequence,

       never *compiled* it — P-LIVE-012's gap in its purest form, found by the first

       default-features = false }` with **no serde feature**, and the nine ULID-backed

      than only `NO_LINK_FILES`, since a broken fence is a rendering defect wherever it
      sits — and watched failing before it was trusted, four ways: the real defect
      reintroduced, a closing fence deleted, an unclosed fence appended to a plan doc, and
      the check run against `HEAD`'s spec (which it fails, naming the line). **The lesson is
      the one this board keeps re-learning in a new costume**: a reviewer reading the spec
      reads *prose*, and a rendering defect is invisible to that act — the reviewer of a
      3 000-line spec is not going to notice that one region is monospace. Where a defect
      class is invisible to the review that is actually performed, the gate is the only
      thing that will ever find it. Appendix G's `check-links.py` row now says three
      invariants and records why the third is not bound to the same file list.

### From the g72 review of the three designed types (session 19, second pass)

The handover from session 18 flagged three protocol types as **designed rather than
transcribed** — `CloseReason`, `Preview`, `TurnView`/`CallView` — and asked for a second
pair of eyes before M1.2 fixtures them, because no gate can tell whether a variant set is
the right one. The review is recorded here rather than only in the tracker because two of
the three changed something. **Verdicts: `Preview` stands unchanged — the one refinement
the review wanted (that `text` is cut on §4.3's head/tail model, so the elision is in the
*middle* and `truncated: bool` does not say where) is already in design §3.2's own comment,
and a `PreviewKind` added later is additive with `Other` as the fallback; `CloseReason` is
missing a producer (U109); and `TurnView` has a data-loss defect (U108).** ✅ **The user
took both recommendations the same day, so both items are closed and their edits are in the
spec** — and the question asked before approving them (*does this mean reverting work
already done?*) is answered with a count in U108's closure: nothing was reverted, nothing
is owed back, and both were forward edits to shapes that had never been compiled.

- [x] **U108 · `TurnView` cannot hold a turn with more than one text block, and the fold
      rule as written destroys the first one — ✅ CLOSED 2026-09-19, option (a) applied.** Three spec sites assume one block and none
      says so: §3.2's `TextEnded { turn, text }` carries "the whole text block"
      (singular); §3.5's `TurnView.text: String` is commented "the whole `TextEnded`
      block"; and §3.2's fold rule says the boundary **replaces** "a block's accumulated
      text" — a phrase with no referent, since a single `String` field cannot distinguish
      one block from the next. `TurnView.thinking: Option<String>` makes the same
      assumption for reasoning.
      **Why more than one block happens.** §6's `StreamChunk` is a *flat* sequence —
      `Text`, `Thinking`, `ToolCallBegin/Args/End`, `Usage`, `Done`, `Failed` — with no
      block index and no end-of-block chunk, so one completion may carry text, a tool call,
      and more text; with interleaved thinking it carries `Thinking → Text → ToolCall →
      Thinking → Text`. That is ordinary provider behaviour, not an edge case. §4.2 makes
      each completion one turn, so the blocks land inside a single `TurnId`.
      **The consequence is durable-state loss, not a rendering nit.** With one accumulator,
      the second `TextEnded` of a turn replaces the first, and because deltas are `Live`
      and never persisted (§3.2), nothing on disk can recover what was replaced. Replay
      from the log reproduces the loss. And whoever writes `fold` first chooses between
      replacing (loses a block) and appending (breaks the duplicate-delta self-heal §14.1
      tests), and the fixture then pins whichever they picked — **U100's own failure mode,
      "a decision taken silently by whoever writes the first `enum`", in a doc that had
      already been promoted.**
      **Three options.** **(a) Recommended: `TurnView.blocks: Vec<TurnBlock>`** with
      `TurnBlock { Text(String), Thinking(String), Call(CallView) }`, and §3.2's rule
      reworded from *replaces* to *closes the open block, replacing its accumulated text*
      — a delta accumulates into the open block, `*Ended` closes it, and a delta after a
      close opens a new one. **No block index is needed on the events**, which is the part
      a reader will ask about: the close is authoritative, so the self-heal property
      survives verbatim, and a *dropped* close is already covered by §3.7's gap detection
      (a durable envelope lost from the live stream is a `seq` discontinuity, so the client
      resyncs rather than folding a merged block). `text`/`thinking` become filters over
      `blocks`, which is two lines of client code. **(b)** Keep `text: String` and require
      the engine to merge a turn's text blocks before emitting `TextEnded` — no type
      change, but the transcript loses where text sat relative to its calls, which is what
      a review UI actually shows ("I'll read X" → call → "X says Y" collapses into one
      paragraph above all calls), and the merge rule still has to be written into §3.2 or
      the fold is ambiguous. **(c)** Add a block index to the four delta/boundary events
      and make `text: Vec<String>` — widens four wire shapes to buy strictly less than (a).
      **Blast radius is smaller than it looks, which is why now is the cheap moment.** No
      `Event` variant changes, so **no event fixture changes**: only `Snapshot`/`TurnView`,
      which is design §8.2's HTTP payload and not a log record, plus §3.2's wording and
      §3.5's type. After M1.2 it is a wire change with a fixture diff and a §9.1 `protocol.d.ts`
      regeneration; before M1.2 it is one enum.
      **Owner: the user — it changes a signed shape — before M1.2 builds `TurnView`.
      Recommendation (a); doc 03 §3.5 carries the do-not-build-against warning and §3.7 the
      fixture consequence (none, which is the asymmetry that makes this cheap).**
      **Verify:** §3.5's `TurnView` holds an ordered block list (or §3.2 states the merge
      rule (b) requires); §3.2's fold rule says *closes* rather than *replaces* and the
      self-heal argument still holds; a §14.1 test folds a turn whose stream is
      text → call → text and asserts both text blocks survive with their order; the
      duplicate-delta test still passes unchanged.
      ✅ **CLOSED 2026-09-19 — the user took option (a).** The question that prompted the
      decision (*does this mean reverting work already done, and bringing it back later?*)
      has a **measured** answer, and it is neither: nothing was reverted and nothing is owed
      back. `TurnView` and `CloseReason` were added to the spec two commits earlier
      (`bc52e50`) and had never been compiled, fixtured, generated into `protocol.d.ts`, or
      rendered by a client — the spec carried `TurnView` at exactly **two** lines (its own
      definition and `Snapshot.turns`'s comment) and `CloseReason` at two (`SessionClosed`
      and its definition), both counted before editing. Both fixes are therefore **forward
      edits**: `CallView` is unchanged and is *reused* as `TurnBlock::Call`, six of
      `TurnView`'s eight fields survive, and the two replaced (`text`, `thinking`) become one
      `blocks: Vec<TurnBlock>`.
      **What landed.** §3.5's `TurnView` plus a new `TurnBlock { Text, Thinking, Call }` with
      the reason in its doc comment; §3.5's "**Four** types `Snapshot` names" → five (counted,
      not incremented); `Snapshot.turns`'s comment, "merged text" → "ordered blocks"; §3.2's
      fold rule reworded from *replaces a block's accumulated text* to ***closes the open
      block, replacing the text the deltas accumulated***, with the self-heal argument
      restated for close-semantics and the two facts that make a block index unnecessary
      (arrival order *is* block order; a dropped close is a `seq` discontinuity, so §3.7
      resyncs rather than merging); a new §3.2 paragraph stating that **a turn may carry more
      than one text block and more than one thinking block** and why (§6's `StreamChunk` is
      flat and carries no end-of-block chunk, §4.2 makes each completion one turn);
      `CallView`'s comment gaining **match a `ToolResult` by `CallId`, never by position**
      (§4.2 dispatches concurrently, so results arrive in no order a block position
      predicts); and §14.1's Protocol bullet gaining a **fourth** two-tier test — text →
      call → text inside one completion, asserting both blocks survive in order with the call
      between them, which the two single-block tests cannot see.
      **Why it was cheap, recorded so the next shape review is scheduled the same way.** No
      `Event` variant changed, so **no fixture existed to change**, and `Snapshot` is §8.2's
      HTTP payload rather than a log record. The same question after M1.2 would have cost the
      Rust struct, `fold`'s text handling, a route payload and M1.3's `protocol.d.ts` — and
      after M1.11, a TUI that renders `.text`. That is the whole argument for reviewing a
      designed type before the crate that fixtures it, and it worked.
- [x] **U109 · `CloseReason` has no variant for the commonest way a child session ends, and
      §5.3 never says whether it ends at all — ✅ CLOSED 2026-09-19, `Completed` added.** The four variants each name a producer:
      `User` an explicit `CloseSession`, `Superseded` a writer fence, `ParentGone` a parent
      that closed, `Shutdown` a host that exited. **A sub-agent that finishes its task has
      none of them** — §5.3 says the child's final message is returned as the tool result
      and that the parent emits `SubAgentFinished`, but not whether the child session is
      closed, by whom, or with what reason. If it is closed, every variant is wrong; if it
      is not, child sessions accumulate in the session list forever with no state that says
      they are finished.
      **Why this is not symmetric with `Preview`.** Adding a `PreviewKind` later is additive
      on the wire and clients fall back to `Other`; a close with no reason cannot be
      rendered at all, and `SessionClosed` is `Durable`, so the gap is in the log rather
      than in one client's rendering.
      **Recommendation: add `Completed`** — "the session finished the work it was spawned
      to do" — and one sentence in §5.3 closing a child session with it when its final
      message is returned. ⚠️ **The doc comment must say it is child-specific**: a *primary*
      session that finishes goes `AgentIdle(Done)` and stays open for more input (§4.2), so
      emitting `Completed` there would make the session list say a session is over while the
      engine is still accepting messages. §11's exit codes map from `IdleReason` and are
      unaffected either way, which is exactly why nothing else would catch it.
      **Owner: the user (a signed variant set), before M1.2's `SessionClosed` fixture;
      §5.3's sentence is agent work and can ride with it.**
      **Verify:** §3.2's `CloseReason` has a variant for every path that closes a session,
      checked by enumerating the producers rather than by reading the list; §5.3 states when
      a child session closes and with what reason; a §14.1 fixture covers the new variant;
      a test asserts a primary session reaching `AgentIdle(Done)` is *not* closed.
      ✅ **CLOSED 2026-09-19 — `Completed` added, with the child-specific rule written into
      §5.3 where the producer lives rather than only into a comment on the variant.** The
      enum's five variants now each name a producer, established by **enumerating the paths
      that close a session** rather than by reading the list: an explicit `CloseSession`, a
      task that finished, a writer fence, a parent that closed, a host that exited. §5.3 now
      states that a child session **is** closed when its final message is returned — which it
      previously never said, so the alternative to a new variant was child sessions
      accumulating in the session list forever with no state marking them finished. §5.3 also
      carries the ⚠️ that makes the variant safe: a *primary* session that finishes goes
      `AgentIdle(Done)` and stays open (§4.2), §11's exit codes map from `IdleReason` rather
      than `CloseReason`, and the fold renders whatever it is given — so a leak would be
      invisible except to a user reading a session list. §14.1's Engine bullet gains the
      paired test (a primary session at `AgentIdle(Done)` emits **no** `SessionClosed`; a
      sub-agent whose final message is returned closes with `Completed`). **`SessionClosed`'s
      fixtures are writable at M1.2 with five variants**, which is the sequencing consequence
      this item was filed ahead of U108 for.

### From the M1.2 pre-flight (session 20)

- [ ] **U110 · The user's stated end-state: serde derives in the shipped crates are
      *eventually* replaceable by a dacode-json-native typed layer — recorded so the
      intent survives, not scheduled.** Filed from the M1.2 dependency question
      (2026-09-20): asked whether §13.3 rested on a misunderstanding (*"I suppose we
      would use serialize/deserialize from the dacode-json"*) and whether serde could
      later be drop-in replaced. **The clarification, measured in the sibling checkout
      the same day:** today those are the same thing — dacode-json's typed layer *is*
      serde (default features `["std","serde"]`; §13.3's own reason line says "serde is
      what the crate's public API is built from"), so §13.3 as signed is accurate rather
      than a misunderstanding. The serde-*free* surfaces are the dynamic layer
      (`Doc`/`Value`/`RawJson` — no typed structs, no derives) and `flat::typed`, whose
      `FlatSchema` was measured as **fixed-stride slots for scalars/`str`/`[str]` only —
      no enums, no nesting, no tagging, and no derive macro yet** (`flat_struct!` is the
      macro_rules stand-in; the module's own docs anticipate a `derive`-feature-gated
      macro later). It cannot express `Event`/`Command` at all today. **The decision
      taken now:** serde as a direct `dacode-protocol` dependency (M1.2), which M1.3's
      JSON-Schema export needs anyway (schemars is serde-based, and §13.3 already
      confines it to an offline generator that never ships). **The intent recorded for
      later:** if dacode-json grows a native typed layer, the serde derives may be
      replaced by it. **Preconditions, so a future session evaluates rather than
      rediscovers:** (1) that layer covers §13.2's encoding conventions — adjacent
      tagging, `Option` omitted, base64 bytes, canonical byte-stable output — with a
      derive; (2) a JSON-Schema export route that does not need runtime serde; (3) a
      sweep of every shipped crate's derives and `#[serde(…)]` attributes. **The safety
      net is M1.2 itself:** all 80 golden fixtures must pass *byte-identical* through
      such a migration (any diff is a compatibility event and proves the migration is
      not semantics-preserving), the boundary diff and `dep-audit.py` show serde leaving
      the shipped graph, and doc 03 §3.7's route-1 macro table means the `Event`/
      `Command` enums and their derive emission live in exactly one place. A migration
      would amend §13.3's *means* while keeping §13.2's per-surface split and §13.4's
      byte-exactness intact — so it is a design delta with a fixture gate, not a
      refactor nobody voted on. **Owner: nobody until a precondition exists; check when
      dacode-json grows a derive feature.**
      **Verify:** the item closes only on an explicit decision — either a design delta

      specified — ruled (b) by the user and applied to §3.6 and §12, 2026-09-21.** §3.6 fixes the durability

      *opener* does when the tail is a partial line — reachable whenever a
      `write_all` larger than the buffer is interrupted between syscalls, or a
      crash lands mid-flush. Appending there would splice a new record onto the
      fragment's line, and since the cursor is position-derived that silently
      renumbers every later record, which is exactly §3.6's "quiet" failure
      class. **A1 refuses the open** (`StoreError::TornTail`) rather than
      repairing, because repair means rewriting a file the append-only rule
      protects and nobody has ruled on it. The alternative — truncate to the
      last newline, the same WAL move `index.bin` already gets — is defensible
      (a fragment was never a record, so nothing readable is lost) and is what
      a user would probably expect, but it is a *log* rewrite and needs a
      decision rather than an implementer's default. **Gates:** nothing today;
      a session that crashed mid-write cannot be reopened until it is answered.
      **Ruled: option (b) — truncate to the last complete newline-terminated line,
      fsync, proceed, and report the discarded byte count to the caller.** The user's
      reasoning was that failing is the worse option and loses more, which is the
      argument the item's own (a) row could not answer: §3.6's design has the *kernel*

      lossy is that the cursor is store-assigned on a *successful* append** — a
      fragment was never acknowledged with one, so no client holds a reference to
      anything removed. It is also §12's validate-and-truncate recovery for
      `index.bin` applied to the file the index projects, so it is consistency rather
      than a new idea. ⚠️ **The one thing this had to state explicitly, because
      AGENTS.md's Never-Do list says "never rewrite or drop event-log entries":** an

      asymmetry is untouched, and §3.6 now says so in terms rather than leaving the

- [x] **U121 · `index.bin`'s on-open validation recovered a *crash* and not a
      *corruption*, and the difference was measured by M1.4 Pass A1's primary
      review rather than argued.** Doc 05 §5.5's invariant 3 said "validate **the
      last record** against the log and truncate to the last good one", and the code
      transcribed it faithfully — walking back from the tail to the first record
      that validates and accepting everything before it **unlooked-at**, on a stated
      assumption that "the corruption model is a lost *suffix*". That is true of a
      crash, because the projection is written after the log, and false of a
      corruption, which is not suffix-shaped. ⚠️ **The consequence inverts the
      asymmetry §12 says decides which file is the truth**: a damaged offset in the
      *middle* of the projection survives the tail check untouched and then
      renumbers the log. Measured with three probes — one index record
      `{seq:1, offset:0}` over a three-record log made the `LogHeader` cursor 1 and
      turned a healthy log unbootstrappable (`range(Cursor(0))` → `CorruptRecord`);
      a middle offset nudged one byte into its line was served as-is and reported
      clean; and, sharpest, a **last** record whose offset names another *legal* line
      start assigned the next append a cursor two past the log's real length, so two
      cursors became phantoms nothing ever carried, `LogRecovery` reported clean at
      every step, and the damage persisted across a reopen. That is §3.6's quiet
      failure verbatim — *"§3.7's gap detection would report phantom
      discontinuities and clients would resync forever"* — arriving from a
      *rebuildable projection* in a single-writer session. **The existing tests
      missed it because all three corruption fixtures were ones validation
      rejects** (all-`0xff`, an offset past EOF, a mid-line offset as the last
      record); nothing tested a corrupt offset that still looks legal, or a corrupt
      record that is not last. **Ruled and applied to doc 05 §5.5**: the tail check
      is necessary and not sufficient, and what closes the gap must stay cheap
      enough for the index to be worth having — verifying every record at open costs
      a seek each, and verifying them in one forward pass costs a full sequential
      read, which is what a rebuild costs, so at that point the index has bought
      nothing. The rule is therefore **O(1) verification at the two points of use**
      (an `append` checks the last index record really names the log's last complete
      line *before* assigning the next cursor; a `range` read compares the `seq`
      inside the record it decoded against the one it was asked for) **plus an
      in-memory arithmetic sweep** of the surviving prefix at open. **Verify:** all
      three probes become tests asserting `tail()` and a clean `range(Cursor(0))`;
      `cargo test -p dacode-core` green with open still sub-linear in the log size;
      doc 05 §5.5's invariant 3 carries the rule. ✅ **Discharged in Pass A1's fix
      round, and the primary review mutation-proved each layer itself rather than
      accepting the claim** (M1 removes the `header_end` floor → probe A's two tests
      fail; M2 removes the sweep → probe G's fails and nothing else; M3 removes the
      decoded-`seq` compare; M4 removes the rebuild-and-retry → probe C's fails). All
      three probes are tests in `store/corruption.rs`, each written against a fixture
      the *old* code accepted — which is the property that separates them from the
      three pre-existing corruption fixtures, all of which validation already
      rejected and so proved nothing. **Sub-linearity is proved structurally rather
      than by timing**: `sweep`'s signature takes no `File`, so it *cannot* perform
      I/O, and `open_does_not_verify_every_record_against_the_log` uses probe C's
      fixture to show open accepting a middle record `validates` would have rejected
      in one seek, with `dropped == 0`. The implementer's refusal to write a timing
      test was right — it would have measured the wrong axis and flaked. ⚠️ **One
      consequence worth keeping: the fix found a second instance of the same class.**
      `jsonl.rs`'s `until - window.from` was unguarded, and in **release** it does
      not panic — `take` wraps, becomes `read_to_end`, and the limit `break`
      truncates to the *right* record, so `read_range` returns `Ok` with exactly the
      envelope asked for. A production caller accepts it, never learns the projection
      lied, never triggers the rebuild, and leaves the damaged `index.bin` on disk.

      of all eight production subtractions in `store/` found the other six provably
