      self-describing", "each carries its own codec tag", because it lives outside
      the log and cannot inherit `LogHeader`) but never the *shape*. *(The quoted
      "always" is the property as it stood when this item was filed; **U125 below
      overturned it** the same day, so a blob is compressed *by policy* and plain
      under `off`. The shape this item pinned is unaffected — only the codec tag's
      value varies.)* A2's
      `FsBlobStore` chose `{"type":"BlobHeader","data":{"codec":"zstd"}}` + `\n` then
      the raw zstd frame — a tagged head record over the compressed bytes, following
      the `LogHeader`/§13.5 convention so the head is self-describing and a future
      codec is a new tag value. **Both reviewers ruled it sound and store-private**:
      `BlobStore::get` returns the *decompressed* bytes and §8.2 serves those, so no
      `Event`, wire frame or golden fixture pins the container and changing it is
      **not** a compatibility event — AGENTS.md's "ask first" does not fire. It is
      recorded in doc 05 §5.3's obligation 4 and in `blob.rs`. The §12 sentence the
      primary asked for is **added**: it names the container (the tagged head record
      over the payload, compressed or plain per U125), records it as **store-private**
      (no `Event`/wire/fixture pins it, so changing it is not a compatibility event),
      and states the two subtleties — a blob is the **only non-rebuildable** artifact
      in a session directory, and `BlobHeader` carries no `format_version` (the `type`
      tag does that job). Doc 05 §5.3's obligation 4 now cites §12 as normative rather
      than owing it. **Verified:** design §12 names the shape; `check-links.py` exit 0
      both modes after.

      so the spec is no longer ahead of it.** The original wart: §3.6/§12 and doc 05 §5.3 all said blob

      compresses only blobs — `"off"` and `"blobs"` produced identical bytes and the

### From the user's feature requests — agent lifecycle control (session 22)

> **Three requested features that form one cluster** — controlling and observing a
> running agent tree from the TUI/web UI in server mode. They share substrate (U127's
> "pause/suspend" action *is* U126's mechanism; U127's "change model" action *is*
> U128) and should be **designed together**, not in isolation. None gates current
> work — they are backlog for the loop, sub-agent and server rows — and each needs a
> design pass before it is transcription, because each adds observable state that
> principle 2 then requires to be an `Event` and a fold.

- [ ] **U126 · User-initiated pause/resume that propagates through the agent tree —
      a global control with a per-agent tristate, requested for server mode (TUI and
      web UI).** ⚠️ **Distinct from everything the spec already calls "pause"** — the
      name is taken twice and a third meaning must not collide: §4.2's
      `StopReason::Paused` / `GuardKind::PauseContinuations` is the *provider's*
      non-terminal pause (oh-my-pi's `pause_turn`, capped by
      `loop.max_pause_continuations`), and §4.1's `CancellationToken` is *terminal*
      (cancel keeps the partial turn with `stop: Cancelled` and cannot be undone).
      This is a third thing: a **resumable user control**. The user's shape:
      - **Tristate per agent: `PENDING_PAUSE` / `PAUSED` / `RESUMED`.** A pause is
        global but reaches agents in order — **upper agents in the workflow are marked
        `PENDING_PAUSE`**: they stop taking *new* input and wait for their children to
        finish the current turn, rather than being halted mid-flight.
      - **An agent is paused at one of two points**, and which one decides what is
        queued: (a) **completing a tool run** (local actions) — the tool's output is
        **queued for the next resumed turn**; (b) **awaiting the provider answer** — in
        `PENDING_PAUSE` the agent still *receives* the answer but runs **no tool
        invocation**, and the next turn is **queued for resume**.
      - **On resume the order matters** — the user proposes **deepest sub-agents
        first** and explicitly asks for other ideas. ⚠️ **Open design question, not a
        settled rule**: deepest-first has an argument (a child's queued turn unblocks
        its parent's wait), but so do shallow-first and queued-input-order; it
        interacts with §5.3's parent-waits-for-child shape and with the (a)/(b)
        queues. A design session must decide it.
      Being observable, every transition must be an **`Event`** and the pause state a
      **fold** of the log (principle 2), so a reconnecting *and* a replaying client
      reconstruct who is paused/pending and what is queued — and the queue itself must
      live somewhere durable-or-reconstructable, not only in a server map (the §8.4 /
      doc 07 §7.7 lesson: state in the log cannot live only in a server map). Touches
      the loop (§4.2), sub-agents (§5.3), the protocol (§3 — new `Pause`/`Resume`
      commands + a pause-state event), the server (§8, propagation in server mode) and
      both clients. Needs a **design session** — fold into or follow the M1.9 loop
      brainstorm, since pause-at-a-turn-boundary is a loop concern; the resumption
      order and the queue's durability are the two questions that session must answer.
      **Verify:** the design records the tristate semantics, the two pause points, the
      queue's home, the resumption order and the (non-colliding) name; §4.2/§5.3/§3
      spec text or a delta follows; this item closes citing them.
- [ ] **U127 · Surface failed agents/sub-agents in the TUI and web UI with recovery
      actions — retry, change model, or pause/suspend (the pause propagating to the
      rest of the agents).** The protocol already carries the seam: `Event::Error {
      message, retryable }` (§3.2, `Live`) with doc 04 §4's rule that a client decides
      on `retryable`; §6/doc 13 retry the provider on 429/5xx with backoff; and A4 made
      a context overflow a *retryable* error with a defined path. What is **new** is the
      **per-agent failure surface and its action menu**: when an agent or sub-agent
      fails, the UI shows it as failed (not merely an inline error chip) and offers
      (a) **retry**, (b) **change model** (→ U128), (c) **pause/suspend** — where pause
      is U126's mechanism and **propagates to the rest of the agents**, so a failure in
      one branch can freeze the workflow rather than let siblings run on. Open
      questions for design: what `retry` re-runs (the provider call, the whole turn, or
      the failed tool — §4.2's turn model and the `retryable` flag bound what is even
      retryable); how a failed *sub-agent* surfaces to its parent (`SubAgentFinished`
      carries the summary via the parent's `ToolResult` per §5.3 — does a failure ride
      the same path, and does the parent retry or escalate?); whether retry is
      automatic (provider-level, already specified) or only user-initiated (this item);
      and the UI affordance (a failed-agent panel with per-agent actions, in both
      clients). **Depends on U126 and U128**, so design the three together. Touches
      §4.2 (the loop's error path), §6 (provider retry), §3 (`Event::Error`, possibly a
      retry command), §5.3 (sub-agent failure), §9.2 (TUI) and §8.2 (web). **Verify:**
      the design records the action set, what retry re-runs and the sub-agent failure
      path; spec/protocol text follows; this item closes citing them.
- [ ] **U128 · Temporary model change per (sub-)agent session, for when a model is
      temporarily unavailable — driven from the UI by navigating to the agent and
      clicking its model name, effective on the next turn, with a cache warning.**
      ⚠️ **The protocol seam already exists — extend it, do not reinvent it**: §3.3
      has `SetModel { session, model }` and A27 added `SettingsChanged { model?,
      agent?, perm_mode? }` (§3.2), which folds into `Snapshot.model` ("seeded by
      `SessionCreated`, updated by `SettingsChanged`"). A *session-level* model change
      is therefore already specified. What is **new**: (a) **per-sub-agent** granularity
      — a sub-agent is a child session (§5.3), so `SetModel` on the child's `SessionId`
      may already reach it, but the *navigation* (pick an agent/sub-agent in the tree)
      and the affordance (click the model name) are not built; (b) **"temporary"** —
      revert-after-N-turns, revert-on-success, or just "until changed back"? The user's
      framing ("a model temporarily unavailable") suggests an auto-revert once the
      original is reachable, a behaviour the spec does not have; (c) **effective next
      turn**, with a **warning that the new message carries no prompt cache for the new
      model** — a §13.4 consequence (the cached prefix is per-model, so a switch starts
      cold) and a UI affordance, not a protocol change; (d) it interacts with **U115**
      (the interim `AgentConfig`/`ModelRef` M1.4 carries, whose replacement M2's doc 17
      owes) — a per-sub-agent model override *is* a `ModelRef` question, so U128 and
      U115 must be reconciled when doc 17 is deepened rather than designed twice.
      Touches §4.1 (`Session.model`), §3.3 (`SetModel`), §5.3 (sub-agent config),
      §13.4 (the cache warning), §9.2/§8.2 (the click affordance). Pairs with U127 (its

      semantics, the per-sub-agent path (reusing `SetModel`/`SettingsChanged`), the
      cache warning and the U115/`ModelRef` reconciliation; spec/protocol text follows;

> exist), and a code comment names no row that will ever read it. The primary's rule for the second one is
> worth keeping: **a deferral is legitimate when its reason is a cost, and illegitimate when its reason is

- [ ] **U137 · Two of the replay pump's five raced `.await`s are unpinned, and the seam to pin them is

      the live `recv` (`a_live_phase_pump_also_ends_on_the_session_token`), and the live `send`
      (`a_live_send_blocked_on_a_stalled_subscriber_ends_on_the_session_token`, which is the one that
      matters most because it is the state the pump actually spends its life in: blocked on a subscriber

      and the failure report's `tx.send(Err(..))` at `replay.rs:392-404`. Both sites say so in the code
      and point at this item.

      never answers; the second needs one that fails on a *later* chunk after ≥`SUBSCRIBER_QUEUE_DEPTH`
      successful deliveries, so the report's send meets a **full** queue — reachable, because `read_cold`
      delivers as it goes and `JsonlStore::read_range` returns `CorruptRecord` for a damaged *middle*
      record (retried once, then surfaced). Neither double exists in the crate: `store::writer::backends`'

      fields `pub` (`:131-139`), `EventStore` (`store/traits.rs:30`) and `LogWriter::spawn` (`:302`) are

- [ ] **U138 · The asker is woken before the `Ack` that tells the client its answer was accepted, so a
      client can see the asker's next event at a *lower* `seq` than the event that unblocked it.**
      `actor.rs`'s `decide_answer`/`decide_resolve` consume the waiter and send on the oneshot during
      **decide**, before the reply is sent at `apply` — and design §3.3's ordering rule is that the `Ack`
      precedes the resulting events. The early decide is **sound and deliberate**: it is what makes
      first-answer-wins race-free, since two concurrent answers must not both reach the waiter. What is
      unstated is the consequence — the woken asker's next `emit` races `apply`'s, so its `ToolResult` can
      land at a lower `seq` than the `QuestionAnswered` that unblocked it, **and before the answering
      client's own `Ack`**. Found by the primary's round-2 review (L5) and recorded on `decide_answer`'s doc,
      cross-referenced from `decide_resolve`, rather than left implicit.
      **Not fixed at C2 because the fix is not local:** removing the entry in `decide` while deferring the
      oneshot send to `apply` needs a **two-phase `PendingRequests` API**, which rewrites C1's
      mutation-proved delivery methods for a caller that does not exist until M1.9. **Exposure at M1.4 is
      nil**: there is no asker — the agent loop is M1.9's, so nothing is ever woken. **Owner: M1.9's loop
      row**, which is the row that creates askers and therefore the first one for which the inversion is
      observable. **Verify:** M1.9 either lands the two-phase API and a test that the asker's next event
      carries a `seq` above the resolution that unblocked it, or records why the inversion is acceptable —
      and this item closes citing whichever. ⚠️ Do not "simplify" the early decide away: it is load-bearing
      for first-answer-wins, and the fix is to move the *send*, not the *decision*.

### From M1.1d (session 27)

> **One hole the pre-flight found by reading §6 against §4.5 and §5.1, and it is the reason doc 13 keeps its
> depth marker.** M1.1d's other two collisions were both *rulable* and were ruled with the user (the client
> stack, g84; `CompletionRequest`'s `ToolSpec` dependency, g85), and a third was ruled from spec facts without
> asking — the SSRF seam, because §4.4 already says the check runs after resolution and hyper-util's resolver
> is where "after resolution" is structural rather than a convention. This one is not rulable, because every
> answer is somebody's product decision rather than a derivation, and one of the three edits normative §6.
> Filed rather than invented, which is what §1's condition (1) asks for: land the approved shape, mark the
> pending content with its owner named.

- [x] **U140 · `ModelInfo.window` has no specified source for a model nobody tabled, and M1.6 consumes it one
      row after M1.5 builds it.** §6 declares `window: u32` **non-optional** — commented *"context window in
      tokens (§4.5's threshold is a fraction of this)"* — and §4.5's `compact_at` is a fraction of the model
      window, so the context row reads a number the provider row must produce. Three spec facts collide:
      **(1)** config resolution is **M2** ([17](part3-capabilities/17-config-agents-skills.md)), so at M1.5
      there is no "user-overridable table in config" to consult, and U115's widening already established there
      are **no built-in defaults** either (§5.1's layer 1 says "built-in defaults (embedded)" and names none);
      **(2)** §6 promises `openai-compat` covers Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio and z.ai **"via base URL"**, which
      means *arbitrary local model names* — so refusing any model absent from a seed table would break the
      only reason that provider exists; **(3)** therefore `window` has no source for an untabled model, and
      inventing one feeds §4.5's threshold a number nobody chose.
      **The pricing half of this hole is CLOSED, from spec facts rather than a decision, and the route is worth
      keeping.** §3.2's `TurnFinished` carries `cost_usd: Option<f64>`, so *absent* is expressible; read
      against §6's own *"a wrong cost is worse than an absent one, because it is believed"*, the rule follows
      without invention: **a model with no known pricing yields `cost_usd: None`, never `0.0`** — a zero cost
      is a believed wrong number, `None` is the truth. That is recorded in doc 13 §13.11 and removes the
      pressure to invent a price table. `window` is the half that stays open, because `u32` has no absent case.
      **Three candidate answers, each somebody's decision:** **(a)** refuse an untabled model — honest, and
      breaks §6's base-URL promise; **(b)** query the provider's `/v1/models` — OpenAI-compatible servers do
      serve model ids, but **not** context windows or pricing, so it cannot fill `window`; **(c)** carry the
      unknown — make `window` optional or add a documented conservative fallback, either of which is a
      **normative §6 edit** and therefore Ask-First. The evidence points at (c), since §4.5 needs *a* number,
      but the fallback value is a product decision with a two-sided failure: too small and compaction fires
      constantly, too large and §4.5's guard never does.
      **Not blocking M1.5's code**, and the reason is a build-order fact rather than a deferral: `complete()`

- [ ] **U154 · One of Pass E's ten conversions is not a timeout at all, and its failure mode is a *silent
      false pass* rather than a hang — which is the one shape this milestone keeps finding and the only one
      no gate sees.** `crates/dacode-core/src/replay_tests.rs:604` waits with an unconditional
      `tokio::time::sleep(SETTLE)` (`SETTLE` = 50 ms, `:58`) and then asserts `extra.is_none()` — an
      **absence window**: it proves nothing arrived, so it can only ever be *widened*, never bounded. Nine of
      the ten loops became `tokio::time::timeout` over a predicate, whose failure is loud (the bound elapses
      and the message says what it was waiting for). This one's failure is the opposite: **if 50 ms is too
      short on a loaded machine, the thing it waits to *not* happen has not happened yet, and
      `assert!(extra.is_none())` passes vacuously.** The test then reports green while asserting nothing.
      ⚠️ **This is not hypothetical for this repo.** M1.4 Pass C2 shipped a ~1.6 % flake with *every* gate
      green, and the second flake it introduced pointed the **other** way — a bound spent by the *observer*
      rather than consumed by the *observed*, failing 8/160 at eight concurrent workers with 1- and 2-worker
      runs clean. A 50 ms absence window is the same coupling: its adequacy depends on host load, and the
      CONTENTION gate is exactly the run that would expose it — but a *vacuous pass* is invisible to a gate
      that counts failures, because there is no failure to count.
      **Why Pass E did not fix it:** the pass was scoped to retiring yield loops, and this one is a genuine
      fourth shape rather than a conversion ("absence is not a predicate", as the code comment says). The
      primary mutation-probed the neighbouring dedupe predicate and recorded `SETTLE` = 50 ms as
      *sufficient* — but "sufficient on this host at this load" is not a property, it is an observation, and
      doc 13 §13.8 now records that this crate's own yield costs moved **33×** between milestones on one
      machine with no load change.
      **Verify:** either (a) the window is made *failable* — assert something that must become true within it,
      so too short a window fails loudly instead of passing vacuously — or (b) its adequacy is measured across
      the CONTENTION gate's load range and recorded beside `SETTLE` with the load stated, per §13.8's rule
      that any bounded wait says **what it gates on**. Whichever is taken, a mutation must prove it: shortening
      `SETTLE` toward zero has to *fail*, and if it does not, the assertion is vacuous today.
      Owner: **whoever next touches `replay_tests.rs`** — which is **U137's split** (`replay_cancel_tests.rs`),

### From M1.5 Pass D

- [ ] **U155 · §6's `ExchangeRecord.response` is `RawJson` — one validated JSON document — and a v1 response

      row): the field's type and the clients' own wire disagree, and no prior ruling covers it — §13.6's four
      obligations bind *how* bodies are recorded (byte-exact, redacted) but never faced the container
      question, and obligation 1 forbids inventing fields. **The disclosed interim, landed rather than
      blocked** (the pass could not defer its own deliverable, and every arm below is a *reader* decision):
      a body that **is** one JSON document is spliced verbatim (byte-identical to the wire — the strongest
      form of obligation 2, and the case §13.4's caching-comparison argument is about, which lives on the
      *request* side); a body that is **UTF-8 text but not JSON** — every SSE stream both v1 clients can
      produce — is carried as a JSON **string** whose decode is the exact body bytes, a container and not a
      re-serialisation (§3.6's "bytes base64" is the house precedent for container-encoding bytes a JSON
      field cannot hold; the string form keeps the diagnostic copy human-readable, which is its whole
      purpose); a body that is **neither** is refused with an `Exchange` error rather than lossily
      converted — unreachable through both v1 clients (their frames are JSON inside ASCII SSE framing), and
      loud rather than silent if a future provider breaks that. `exchange.rs`'s module header and doc 13
      §13.6's Pass D addendum carry the shape; `an_sse_body_travels_in_the_lossless_string_container` and
      `a_non_utf8_non_json_body_is_refused_rather_than_corrupted` pin both halves.
      **Which arm:** (i) ratify the container — M5's analyzer decodes the string when the field is not an
      object, and §6's comment gains one sentence (Ask-First: a normative edit); (ii) amend §6's field type
      (bytes-with-encoding, or a document-or-text sum) — Ask-First, a protocol-adjacent shape change with a
      golden-fixture question beside it; (iii) record the response as an assembled JSON array of the
      frames' `data` documents, each spliced byte-exact — friendlier to the analyzer, but it drops the SSE
      envelope bytes and so weakens "the body received" to "the payloads received", which needs the same
      Ask-First as (ii). **Verify:** M5's analyzer row (doc 25) and M1.9's wiring name the shape they read
      rather than rediscovering it; if (i), §6's comment edit lands in the analyzer's commit; the interim's
      two pins above stay until whichever arm lands. Owner: **M5's analyzer row, with M1.9's wiring as the
      first reader** — whoever touches the field first. It gates no milestone build, so `attention.py`'s

### From M1.1e (session 36)

- [x] **U156 · §4.5's `Segment.digest: [u8; 32]` names no hash function, and no hashing crate is a
      `dacode-core` edge — so `Segment` is not constructible and M1.6 cannot start.** Filed by M1.1e's
      field-by-field walk over §4.5; [09](part2-engine/09-context-caching.md) §9.5 carries the arms and the
      measurement. **Measured, not recalled**: the design names no hash anywhere (`rg -n
      'digest|SHA-256|sha2|blake3' docs/dacode-design.md` returns only §4.5's own field and its prose about
      fingerprints); `dacode-core`'s nine normal edges are `fd-lock`, `serde`, `zstd`, `tokio`,
      `tokio-util` plus the four in-workspace crates, and none hashes; the only hash-capable crate in the
      lock is `ring`, which is class-1 and a `dacode-providers` edge; `dacode-json` exposes none (`rg -l
      'sha256|blake3' ../../rust/json-tiers/src` is empty); and `dacode-protocol/tests/corpus.rs` only
      *mentions* a sha256 in two comments (`:100`, `:630`) because it byte-compares — so there is no
      in-tree implementation to reuse either. **This is U117's and U140's shape a third time**: a normative
      field whose value has no specified source, found by walking a section rather than by building
      against it.
      ⚠️ **The reference this technique came from uses a 32-bit non-crypto hash, which is why the arms
      differ in what they buy and not only in price.** oh-my-pi's two digests are both
      `hash = ((hash << 5) - hash + c) | 0` over a `JSON.stringify` of a hand-projected field set
      (`append-only-context.ts:311-334` per message, `:355-374` for the prefix, returning base36), and
      their purpose is **change detection, not integrity** — `StablePrefix.build()` returns a bool
      documented as "true if the prefix actually changed (cache miss imminent)" (`:67-76`). §4.5's 32-byte
      field is a step *beyond* the reference, and only (a)/(b)/(c) fill it with a construction somebody
      else has analysed.
      **Arms** (doc 09 §9.5's table carries the costs and failure modes): **(a) `sha2` 0.10 —
      recommended**; (b) `sha2` 0.11; (c) `ring::digest`, already in the lock but bringing class-1 C/asm
      into a second crate against §2.3's pure-Rust default; (d) a wide in-crate fingerprint (four 64-bit
      lanes with fixed keys, zero dependencies) — **the jitter-xorshift precedent applied to the wrong

      transient allocation, where the backward-scan-from-tail alternative R-h deferred would have been

      `actor_tests.rs` is not a file M1.6 owns, so the pass stated the invariant on `apply`'s own doc and
      filed this rather than editing a neighbour.

      `registry_tests.rs` `take_control` claimed a fence that did not exist (the primary's MED-2,

      the two `actor_tests.rs` tests still fail — which is what makes the one a fence and the other not.
      **Owner: whoever next touches `actor.rs`'s `apply` or `actor_tests.rs`.** **Verify:** either both
      tests fence on a later command's `Ack` the way `registry_tests.rs`'s `take_control` now does, or

      its fixture; (b) `PermissionResolved` gains an `Option<DenyReason>` field beside `by`, which is
      additive and omits when `None` per §13.5's convention, but puts the reason on the *event* rather than
      on the *decision*, so a `Snapshot` that folds decisions without events cannot see it; (c) a separate
      `EgressRefused` event, which makes the two layers structurally distinct at the cost of a fourth
      durable variant and a fold branch. **Recommendation: (a)** — the reason is a property of the denial
      and not of its delivery, §3.2's `PermDecision` already carries a payload variant
      (`AllowPattern(String)`), so this is not the enum's first, and (b)'s `Snapshot` blindness is exactly
      the "a fold cannot match it" failure A3 ruled out. **Verify:** the arm is ruled **before M1.7's first
      commit** and before `event.rs` is touched — ⚠️ which is **998 of the ungated 1 000-line cap**, the
      closest file in the workspace, so a reason-carrying `Deny` does not fit beside it and the row plans a
      split or moves the prose to `snapshot.rs` (the decision M1.6 Pass B had to make and did); the golden
      fixture changes **in the same commit** and is called out as the compatibility event it is; §14.1's
      Providers-tier test #5 gains an assertion that the two layers are *distinguishable*, not only that
      the private-range case is refused, since a test that only asserts the refusal passes on any of the
      three arms and on none of them being implemented. Owner: **the user** for the arm, consumed by
      **M1.7** — **M1 scope**, and the deadline is M1.3's publication rather than M1.7's commit.

- [ ] **U163 · What a session grant does to the *other* pending permission requests is unspecified, and
      two harnesses do opposite things.** §4.4 defines the decision and its audit; §7.3 and doc 07 define
      first-answer-wins delivery for *one* request; nothing says what an `AllowSession` or `AllowPattern`
      means for the requests already waiting. Measured in the checkouts: **opencode auto-resolves every
      pending request its new saved rules now cover** (`packages/core/src/permission.ts:250-259`) and
      **cascades a reject to all pendings in the session** (`:237-245`) — two cross-request rules, both
      load-bearing for a UI where several prompts are open at once. **Nil exposure at M1.7**, and the
      reason is structural rather than incidental: nothing emits a `PermissionRequested` until §4.2's loop
      exists, so at this row the pending set can only ever hold one entry, created by a test. From **M1.9**
      the loop dispatches calls concurrently under §4.3's `Concurrency` policies, so several `ask`
      decisions can be open at once and the question becomes observable — which makes this U139's shape
      (a consequence recorded at the row that creates it, with the time box named) rather than a note.
      ⚠️ **Doc 16 §16.2 states M1.7's behaviour explicitly so the row does not pick one silently**: each
      pending is answered on its own, a new grant does not retro-resolve an older request, and a `Deny`
      does not cascade. That is the *conservative* reading and the one that needs no new surface, but it
      has a cost worth naming when the arm is chosen: a user who answers "allow all `cargo *` for this
      session" while three `cargo` prompts are open still has to answer the other two. **Which arm:**
      (a) as doc 16 states it — independent requests, no retro-resolution; (b) opencode's
      auto-resolve-covered-pendings, which needs the new grant re-run against each waiting scope and a
      rule for which `by` the synthesized `PermissionResolved` carries (the granting client, or `None` as
      an engine resolution — the **event field's own** wording for the timeout case,
      `event.rs:539-540`; ⚠️ this entry first cited §3.2 for it, which is the same misattribution the
      primary review found in `perm.rs` at M1.7 Step 0, and §3.2's only `by` occurrences are the bare
      uncommented declarations at `dacode-design.md:361,363`); (c) auto-resolve for `allow` and
      independent answers for `deny`, on the argument that a denial is a decision about *one* call while a
      grant is a decision about a class. **Verify:** M1.9 names the arm in doc 08 before the loop
      dispatches concurrently, and a test pins it by opening two `ask` pendings and granting a pattern that
      covers both — asserting either that the second resolves with the named `by`, or that it stays open,
      whichever arm is taken; this item closes citing that test. Owner: **M1.9** — **M1 scope**.

- [ ] **U164 · §4.4's `deny_ip_ranges` vocabulary reads as exhaustive and is not, and one of the two
      omissions cannot be std-derived on the pinned toolchain.** §4.4 names four sets —
      `["loopback", "private", "link-local", "metadata"]` — "or CIDR". Measured while establishing that the
      IP layer needs **zero dependencies** (doc 16 §16.8): `Ipv4Addr::is_shared` (CGNAT, `100.64.0.0/10`)
      and `is_benchmarking` are **unstable** on `rustc 1.98.1` (`error[E0658]`, issue #27709), while
      everything the four named sets need is stable — including `Ipv6Addr::is_unique_local`,
      `is_unicast_link_local` and `to_ipv4_mapped`. So a resolved address in CGNAT space is **not
      classifiable by any std name**, and `0.0.0.0/8` is omitted from the list as well. Both are reachable
      by the exact case §4.4 exists to stop: an allow-listed hostname whose DNS answer an attacker
      controls. **Two smaller findings from the same measurement, recorded rather than gated:**
      `169.254.169.254` is `is_link_local()` and is **not** `is_private()`, so the four sets are not nested
      the way a reader assumes and `link-local` is load-bearing rather than redundant beside `metadata`;
      and `::ffff:127.0.0.1` is **not** `Ipv6Addr::is_loopback()` without `to_ipv4_mapped()` first, which
      is a loopback bypass for any implementation that calls only the v6 predicates — the reason
      openclaw's `net-policy` handles mapped and embedded forms explicitly
      (`packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts:190`, whose own comment reads *"including IPv4-mapped IPv6"*). Both
      are pinned by tests in doc 16 §16.8's trap list, so neither is a hole in the *code* — only the
      vocabulary is. **Which arm:** (a) add `cgnat` and `this-host` to the named-set vocabulary — spec
      text, so **Ask-First**, and it makes the list exhaustive against the ranges that matter; (b) leave
      the vocabulary as written and require operators to spell `100.64.0.0/10` as CIDR, which works
      (R-f hand-rolls a CIDR parser) but means the default configuration has a hole the named sets appear
      to close; (c) treat the four names as a *floor* the engine always applies regardless of config, so
      no spelling can remove loopback/link-local/private — the shape openclaw's approval-file floors take.
      **Recommendation: (a) plus (c)** — (a) because a name an operator cannot write is a range an operator
      cannot deny, and (c) because a *deny* list whose defaults are removable by omission is the same
      inversion as §16.4's `.env`. **Verify:** folded into **g129**'s spec edit if the user wants one; if
      not, doc 16 §16.8 names the two omissions as known and M1.7's `[net_policy]` tests pin whatever the
      shipped default actually covers, so the gap is measured rather than assumed. Owner: **the user** for
      the vocabulary, consumed by **M1.7** — **M1 scope**, low severity, and unlike U162 it does not
      become more expensive later because no wire shape depends on it.

- [ ] **U165 · `tools/agents-index.py --check` has no fixpoint, so its exit code carries no information —
      and AGENTS.md's diagnosis of the red was wrong in the direction that hides the case firing most
      often.** Measured at M1.1f (2026-10-01, tracker f311) on a commit that touched **no** `AGENTS.md`:
      the check exited 1, and regenerating produced a diff in **two** columns — the root doc's `lag`
      **4 → 8** with its `rev` unchanged at `3436e81`, and `crates/dacode-core`'s `rev` `55bdc04 →
      915e0d7` with its hash (`dae26a92`) and line count (787L) both unchanged. The mechanism is in the
      tool: `lag = git rev-list --count <doc_rev>..HEAD -- <covered-dir> :!<doc>`
      (`tools/agents-index.py:120`), and the **root** `AGENTS.md`'s covered directory is the repository
      root, so *every* commit increments it. Regenerating and committing the index then moves HEAD, which
      increments it again — **there is no clean tree at which `--check` exits 0**. AGENTS.md said the red
      comes "on the `rev` column alone", which is false for the root row, and is why a reader following
      that instruction sees a delta in a column the instruction says cannot move and then has to decide
      whether the index is stale or the doc is. Corrected in the same change as this item.
      **Why it is more than cosmetic:** the check exists to catch exactly one failure — a hash that was
      never regenerated, which is what shipped at `a8bbd53` — and a gate that is always red is a gate whose
      signal has to be recovered by a manual procedure (regenerate, diff, read the *hash* column). Three
      consecutive sessions have now run that procedure and reverted the file, which is U44's shape, but a
      procedure someone has to remember is the second-class gate the 2026-09-30 correction was made to
      avoid — and this pass is the second time the rememberable half was a *sentence* rather than a
      command. **Which arm:** (a) drop the derived, always-moving columns from `--check`'s comparison —
      compare **hash, line count and `rev`** only and render `lag` as informational — which makes exit 0
      reachable and leaves the check catching precisely the failure it exists for; (b) special-case the
      root doc, whose covered directory is the repo root by construction, so its `lag` measures "commits
      since the last agent-instruction edit" rather than the "doc trailing its code" the column claims;
      (c) leave the tool alone and promote the regenerate-and-diff procedure into `tools/` as a wrapper
      that prints the diagnosis, so the procedure is a command rather than a paragraph.
      **Recommendation: (a), with (b)'s observation recorded beside it** — (a) is a small change that
      restores a signal, and (b) alone would leave `rev` red after any doc-touching commit, which is U44's
      benign case and still not exit 0.
      ⚠️ **Arm (a) as first written is insufficient, and running the procedure is what showed it.** (a) said
      to compare "hash, line count **and `rev`**" — but `rev` **cannot** record the commit that edits the
      doc, because the index is generated *before* the commit that carries the edit. Measured at M1.7 Step 0
      on a tree where `AGENTS.md` had just been committed at `cc3a594`: the committed index said `rev`
      `3436e81` with hash `c57df08f` and 336L, regeneration produced hash `c57df08f` and 336L **unchanged**
      and `rev` `cc3a594` — correct, and uncommittable without moving HEAD again. So `rev` is stale by
      *construction* for exactly the doc the check exists to protect, and (a) would still exit 1 after any
      `AGENTS.md` edit. **Corrected arm (a): compare hash and line count only** — the two columns that
      describe *content* — and render both `rev` and `lag` as informational, since both are derived from
      HEAD and neither can be current at a clean tree. ⚠️ Any arm changes a **gate's semantics**, so it is a decision
      rather than a fix-in-passing, and whichever is taken must land with
      [Appendix G](appendices/G-authoring-tools.md)'s row updated, that register being where §2.4 says a
      tool's contract lives. **Verify:** `agents-index.py --check` exits **0** at a clean tree with no
      `AGENTS.md` edit pending, exits **1** when a hash is stale — proved by editing a doc without
      regenerating, then reverting — and Appendix G's row names what the check compares; this item closes
      citing that pair of runs. Owner: **the user** for the arm — **no milestone impact**, and unlike U162
      it does not become more expensive later.
      ⚠️ **A sibling misrendering measured in the same pass, and it is `attention.py` rather than
      `agents-index.py` — recorded here because both are one defect: a gate whose output is *derived* where
      it should be *declared*.** This item renders **P0 "gates M1"** and it gates no milestone. The cause is
      `_MILESTONE_GATING`'s second alternative (`tools/attention.py:143`), whose preposition list includes
      `at`, so the provenance phrase *"Measured at M1.1f"* matches as a gating construction — the `\b` after
      `M1` holds because `.` is a non-word character, so a **sub-step label is indistinguishable from a
      milestone**. ⚠️ **The naive fix is wrong, and that was measured rather than assumed**: excluding every
      `M(\d)\.\d` would suppress **58** matches in §6, most of which *are* genuinely gating — "owed before
      M1.9 wires a provider" is U148's, and U148 is correctly P0 — so the heuristic's own stated preference
      ("under-triggering is the safe failure") argues against it. The precise gap is narrower: **§6
      milestones are detected from prose while §6 *actions* are declared**, and the `attention-meta` block
      at §6's head already exists for exactly this purpose, its own text reading *"Declared rather than
      detected … applied to the third and last scraped field"* — a claim this item falsifies, since the
      milestone is a fourth scraped field and is still detected (deltas' milestones *are* declarable, at
      `attention.py:342`). **So arm (d): add a `milestone:` line to that block**, mirroring `action:` and the
      Appendix B `confidence-lead:` precedent, with a hygiene check that every declared id exists and every
      value is in `MILESTONE_ORDER`. **Recommendation: (a) plus (d)** — (a) restores a signal to one gate,
      (d) removes a class of false P0 from the other, and neither is the regex surgery the 58-match
      measurement rules out.

- [x] **U166 · §4.4 logs *every* decision on `PermissionResolved` "including automatic ones", but an
      automatic decision has no `PermissionRequested` — so its `ReqId` names nothing.** Found at M1.7 Step 0
      (2026-10-01) while landing U162, and **U162's own shape makes it unavoidable rather than
      theoretical.** Three pieces of normative text do not compose: §4.4's *"Every decision is logged
      (`PermissionResolved`), including automatic ones, so the audit trail is complete"*; §4.3's *"a
      refusal is recorded on `PermissionResolved` like any other denial"*; and §3.2's definition of the id
      those events carry — *"a `ReqId` names a request the **engine made of the user**"*
      (`dacode-design.md:279-281`, with `:233` glossing it "question / permission request"). For an
      automatic decision the engine made no request of the user, so the resolution carries an id whose
      referent was never emitted, and a client that folds the log sees a `PermissionResolved` for a
      `PermissionRequested` that does not exist. **Why U162 forces it:** `DenyReason::NetAddress` is
      produced by the IP layer at **connect** time, *after* the `net` decision already resolved
      automatically as allow — so the denial that most needs recording is precisely one with no request
      behind it. Nothing in the tree can hit this yet (`decide_resolve` only serves a client answer, which
      always has a request), which is why it is filed rather than fixed. **Which arm:** (a) the engine
      mints a `ReqId` for every decision and emits only the resolution, making `ReqId` a **correlation
      handle** rather than the name of an emitted request — needs one spec sentence amending §3.2's
      wording, and nothing else; (b) automatic decisions emit **both** events, so every id names a request
      and the audit trail is uniform — but a `PermissionRequested` nobody was asked is a prompt a UI must
      know not to render, and it doubles the log volume on the *common* path, since most decisions in an
      `auto-edit` or `yolo` session are automatic; (c) automatic decisions are logged on a **new** event
      (`PermissionChecked`), leaving `PermissionResolved` for real answers — which makes §4.4's "recorded
      on `PermissionResolved` like any other denial" false as written, costs a durable variant and a fold
      branch, and ⚠️ lands on `event.rs` at **998 of the ungated 1 000-line cap** (doc 16 §16.13's
      corrected gate 2). **Recommendation: (a)**, because §4.4's requirement is that the *decision* is
      recorded and (a) is the only arm that records it without paying on the common path — and the wording
      it amends is a *definition* of an id type, not a property a client depends on. **Verify:** M1.7 names
      the arm before it emits its first automatic decision; if (a), §3.2's `ReqId` sentence is amended in
      the same commit as the code (§2.3's same-commit rule, applied to spec text) and a fold test pins that
      a `PermissionResolved` with no matching `PermissionRequested` is *accepted* rather than treated as a
      gap; if (b) or (c), the rendering rule and the fixture set move with it. Owner: **M1.7** — **M1
      scope**, and unlike U162 it does not get more expensive at M1.3 unless the arm is (c).
      ✅ **RULED arm (a) by the user 2026-10-03, and CLOSED at M1.7 Pass B in the same commit** — each
      Verify-clause part annotated against a re-measurement: the arm was named *before* Pass B wrote the
      minting (the ruling preceded the dispatch); §3.2's sentence is amended in this commit (the
      correlation-handle wording, `dacode-design.md:279-283`); and the fold test is
      `a_resolution_for_a_request_never_emitted_is_a_no_op` (`tests/fold.rs:602`, dacode-protocol
      125 → 126). `check()` returns the minted `ReqId` beside the decision
      (`check_mints_a_fresh_req_id_for_every_decision_u166`), and no `Event` variant was added — arm (c)'s
      `event.rs` cap hazard never materialised.

- [ ] **U167 · `Domain::Path` does not fold case, so on a case-insensitive filesystem a `deny` is voided
      by spelling — `edit.deny = ["**/.env"]` does not deny `.ENV`, which the filesystem opens as
      `.env`.** Found at M1.7 Pass A's review (2026-10-02) and **ruled arm (a) by the user the same
      day** (R-h, doc 16 §16.15): the matcher stays non-folding, the asymmetry is documented at the site
      (`pattern.rs`'s header), and this item is the filed hole. **Measured, not reasoned:** on this
      machine's default APFS `python3 -c 'os.path.samefile(".env",".ENV")'` is `True` and `open(".ENV")`
      reads a file created as `.env` — §16.4's *worse* direction, a voided `deny`. **Why folding is not
      the fix:** on a case-sensitive filesystem (default Linux) folding converts the voided `deny` into
      a widened `allow` (`src/*` permitting `SRC/secret`), so there is no single correct answer without
      knowing which filesystem the paths are on. **And why the matcher cannot ask:** g128's consequence 1
      makes it a pure predicate over `(Domain, pattern, subject bytes)` with no filesystem access — the
      sandbox-adoptability constraint the user added — so the case-sensitivity must arrive from the caller
      that supplies the `Domain`, which at M1.7 does not exist (Pass B's `scope.rs`) and which itself has
      no filesystem knowledge until config exists. **The fix shape, when doc 17 builds it:** a
      case-sensitivity flag on `Domain` (or a `PathInsensitive` variant) supplied by the config layer,
      which is the only place that knows the filesystem the session's `cwd` is on. **Verify:** doc 17
      cites this item when it designs `[permissions]`'s loading, and the matcher's non-folding test in
      `pattern_tests.rs` is no longer the last word on the behaviour. Owner: **M2 / doc 17**.

The §23.4 sequence test is green — the integration test asserts the stream envelope-by-envelope, byte-identical to the log's prefix — and the sandbox decision is recorded at `engine.rs`'s `create_session` and both crate AGENTS.md files. Closes citing `crates/dacode/tests/run.rs`'s sequence assertion and `engine_tests.rs`' four producer tests.
